maintopic: PURCHASES OF AMERICAN CATTLE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT.
PURCHASES OF AMERICAN CATTLE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Before the Orders of the Day are called, I would ask whether the attention of the govern-

ment lias been directed to the following information published in this morning's Montreal * Gazette ' :
The work of stocking Boer farms in South Africa with American dairy cattle is steadily proceeding, and a lucrative trade is being worked up. The steamer ' Atlantean,' which is now in port loading 2,000 tons of hay as export cargo for South Africa, will go from here to Galveston, Texas, to load dairy cattle for interior points in the Orange River Colony. The cattle are being sent to Africa by the British government to replace those which were either driven off or commandeered by the British during the war.
It is expected that the ' Atlantean ' will carry between 2,000 and 2,500 head of cattle on this trip. This will be her second voyage to South Africa with cattle.
Every animal accepted is subjected to a rigid examination, the utmost care being taken by the British government that all cattle sent to Africa shall be of high class and without a blemish.
For these cattle good prices are being paid, and southern cattle dealers are reaping a harvest in consequence. Great care is, however, exercised in the selection, and instances are known where out of forty or fifty cattle offered only a very small proportion were accepted.
The interests of the British government in the cattle shipping business are being looked after by Major Maude, of Ottawa, and he in turn is represented by Mr. Kirtaw, of New York, who is now at the Windsor, superintending the shipment of the hay cargo on the ' Atlantean.'
When seen last evening Mr. Kirtaw said he was not in a position to speak definitely as to the cattle business, as he was not the official who has charge of the purchasing. He knew, however, that the business had grown to large proportions.
The trade had its inception soon after the end of the war, and as soon as the British government assumed control of African affairs and began to replace the herds of Boer cattle which had been driven away during the war. He expected that the ' Atlantean ' would take about 2.500 head. They would be shipped to the interior of the country and' gradually distributed.
I bring this to the attention of the government because it has occurred to me, from reading this paragraph, that here would be a very good opportunity indeed for the shipping of cattle from Canada, and that this restocking of Boer farms should, to a very considerable extent, be done by Canadian cattle raisers. Has the attention of the government been directed to the subject matter of this paragraph, and have any representations been made to the imperial government, pointing out the desirability of their obtaining shipments of this kind as far as possible from Canada ?	*

maintopic: PURCHASES OF AMERICAN CATTLE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I may say that I was not aware of the statements contained in the paragraph cited, nor of the shipments in question. Immediately after it was announced that the imperial authorities were going to purchase cattle for the restocking of the Boer farms in South Africa most urgent representations were made by this gov-
speakername: The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Hon. Sydney Fisher).

maintopic: PURCHASES OF AMERICAN CATTLE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: eminent, through Lord Strathc'ona, to the imperial authorities that these purchases should be made in Canada, and explanations were given of what Canada could do in the way of supplying the demand. These representations were referred, by the Colonial Secretary of State, to the imperial officers in charge of the work, and we were informed that they would receive due consideration. A second time the attention of the imperial government was called to the fact that large purchases were being made in the United States on the lines indicated by this newspaper paragraph, but so far no attention has been paid by the imperial authorities to these representations.^

maintopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE.
QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE.
speechtext:
I rise, Mr. Speaker, to a question of privilege. On the 18th June instant the question was asked in this House, is J. T. Schell a member of the fil-m of McPherson & Schell ? I may answer in reply to that inquiry, Yes.
The matter to which this inquiry refers is one which arose from an order given by a Mr. Scott to the firm mentioned. The said order was given for one hundred shooks for cheese boxes to be sent to Glasgow, Scotland. The order was given on paper headed 1 Glasgow International Exhibition, 1901.' It was dated Ottawa, February 18th, 1901 ; signed W. D. Scott, Commissioner, per C. H. M. There was nothing to indicate that Mr. Scott was an officer of the Dominion government. In fact the terms of the order as received rather favoured the idea that Mr. Scott was a commissioner from the old country.
The order contained a request that a memorandum of the amount should be sent to Mr. Scott personally, not to any officer or department of the government. I may here state that the sum involved in this transaction is $4, with an additional $1.50 for package. At any rate, the order was received in my absence at Ottawa in the usual course of business, and was attended to by the manager of the business. The firm of which I am a member has before this refused orders which they knew to come from the Dominion government.
If any further evidence is required as to the understanding by our manager that the transaction was one with Mr. Scott personally, I may refer to the invoice, a press copy of which we have in our invoice book, and which is simply In this form :
W. D. Scott, Ottawa, to 100 sets cheese
hoops	$4 00
Crating, &c	 1 50

That same entry was carried through our books and posted in our ledger in exactly the same terms, as a transaction with Mr. Scott personally. The matter was carried

through all our books and, when the payment was made more than a year afterwards, I was again absent from Alexandria, being engaged in attendance on this House, and the receipt of the payment is a simple entry in the cash book credited to Mr. W. D. Scott. The manner in which this payment was made I was not aware of any more than I was of the transaction itself. The first intimation X had of there being any transaction whatever with the Dominion government was the question raised on the 18th of June, as appearing on the Order Paper.
This is a simple and straightforward statement of the whole transaction, and I should say ought to strike any man of common sense as evidence of my entire ignorance of the transaction, and, therefore, of the absence of any intention to infringe upon any law relating to the independence of the members of this House. I submit myself and the whole matter to the judgment of this honourable House.

maintopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE.
speechtext:
I move :
That the statement just read by Mr. Schell, the member for Glengarry, be referred to the Committee on Privileges and Elections.
speakername: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick).

speechtext: Motion agreed to.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I have not read this Bill, but I would ask the minister in regard to fixing the number at fifty cows in order to constitute a creamery, whether butter that is marked dairy butter would imply a lower grade of butter than creamery butter ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I do not think it
speakername: The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Hon. Sydney Fisher).

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: would. The object is to prevent what has been done in certain cases, and which is held to be a detriment to the export trade in butter. There is still in Canada some continuance of a practice which has generally been discontinued, of repacking small lots of butter into boxes or tubs, and marking it ' creamery,' and forwarding it as creamery butter. Now, our creamery butter lias a certain standard, and if butter is not so made, but is marked ' creamery butter,' there is a danger that it will not be up to the reputation which has attached to creamery butter. Complaints have been made to my officers of these packages as damaging the reputation of our creamery butter, therefore, it is that we put in this definition of creamery butter.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I should say that it would be a reflection upon a farmer that had only forty-nine cows, if he was not permitted to mark his butter ' creamery butter,' although it may be made under the regular process of creamery manufacture. He would then come under the odium that might reflect upon butter stamped ' dairy.' The minister says that our butter has been injured to some extent. We should prevent that, but in safeguarding the reputation of our butter in England, we should be careful not to reflect upon a very good quality of butter that is made by individual farmers. After the experience of large dairying, we find now that the labour of carrying large quantities of milk to the factory has become so burdensome in some sections of the country that farmers are starting out with small separators and carrying the cream to the factory, and it is yet to be tested whether cream so collected is not going to produce a really first-class quality of butter. It is possible to collect this cream from large areas and manufacture it into a first-class quality of butter. Since the development of the dairy industry, in many parts of Canada we have to-day herds of fifty cows where we had not more than ten cows before. In passing this Act we should be careful to do nothing that would reflect upon the product of a man who has less than fifty cows, if it should be determined that their milk can be made under the regular creamery process into butter that will perhaps bring the highest price because the milk is not exposed to any other than the first-class conditions provided by the farmer.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
I quite understand the objection the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pope) makes and there is some force in it. When we considered this section we found that we had to adopt a definite number. It would be very difficult in any other way to describe creamery butter. The ordinary acceptance of the term creamery butter is butter that is made in a cooperative factory and not on the individual farm. I understand fully that a great t many private dairies make just as good but-

ter as is made in any creamery or anywhere else in the country, but we certainly must acknowledge that when butter is made in very small lots and packed in a package it is almost impossible that it should have the character that creamery butter ordinarily has, and it was to avoid any such misrepresentation as is likely to occur under the present condition of affairs that we adopted this number as it would not be desirable to have any such butter sent forward under the name of creamery butter. I understand that the number fifty is rather an arbitrary number, but I do not know that we can get a much better number to serve the purpose. If we go much below fifty the dairies would be hardly of the character that the hon. gentleman has just described.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Is that not a good argument for making it a little lower-say twenty-five instead of fifty ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I do not know that I would object if we put it at twenty-five or thirty instead of fifty, although fifty seems to be a very reasonable number. I think, as a matter of fact, that a great deal of dairy butter is sold at as high a price as creamery butter. Where the dairy butter is of the character that the hon. gentleman has described I think it is its reputation that gives it that price, but where the dairy is of a smaller character and the product cannot conform to the necessary uniformity and equality required by the export trade it would hardly be entitled to be marked as creamery butter. I am not particularly wedded to this particular number, but we thought it was as safe a number as we could take.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Fifty cows would have a product sufficient to fill an ordinary package of fifty pounds, which would entitle a creamery to participate in the export trade.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: But perhaps a less number of cows hardly would.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I would suggest that it should be made a less number. .

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
The product of fifty cows kept where the creamery is situated would have a better chance of being converted into good butter than if the product were gathered from different farms and taken to a creamery. The cows would be kept in one place, they would be managed in the same way, and because of that they would produce better quaility of butfier than the butter which would be made from the product of scattered herds. It is too bad if, by reason of this Bill going into effect, butter so made should get the name or the status of a secondary article. If you must give names to the different varieties of butter you must endeavour to find some means whereby you shall not prejudice the
kind of butter that I have spoken of in the minds of those who purchase it. There are farmers who keep about the number of cows that is mentioned in this subsection and who manufacture their own butter on their own farms. I believe that a better class of butter can be made in one dairy from the product of a single herd than can be made from the product of various herds.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I quite sympathize with what has been said by the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Pope) and the hon. member for East Middlesex (Mr. Gilmour) I think, for various reasons and especially for the reasons that these two hon. gentlemen have suggested, that the number fifty in this subsection is too large. I have understood that one of the difficulties in establishing creameries in sections of the country where creameries have not at all become common was to. get a sufficient number of people interested in the matter. I believe that if the law will permit butter made in a creamery with a less number of cows than fifty, to be marked and sold as creamery butter, it will assist people who may be interested in this matter to establish a creamery, where otherwise it would not be easily established, and for that reason and the reasons suggested by these hon. gentlemen I think, on further consideration the proposal I am about to make will meet with the views of the hon. minister. I beg to move that the word ' fifty ' in subsection (a) be struck out and that the word ' twenty-five ' be substituted in lieu thereof.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Make it twenty.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I am not particular whether it is twenty or twenty-five, but I thought it was quite sufficient if I split the number in two. It will then meet the case of a farmer who desires to put in the necessary plant and make creamery butter even if he only has forty or forty-five cows, or a less number than fifty, and it will meet the case of a neighbourhood where no creamery has been established and assist those who would be interested in it and who have perhaps ten, or fifteen cows, in getting a sufficient number to join together to start a creamery which might afterwards be enlarged so as to make an establishment taking the milk of perhaps 200 cows. I think the hon. minister is going to defeat the object he has in view by limiting this number to fifty, and depriving a certain number of people of the privilege in regard to selling their butter to which they are just as much entitled as others living in a section of the country where a larger number of people take an interest in the manufacture of creamery butter or where a farmer desires to enter into the manufacture of butter on his own account.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
Any one who looks at
the market will notice the distinction at

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
The amendment proposed by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) to reduce the figure is certainly worthy of consideration, but I think we ought not to change it without very careful consideration and without a full understanding of the subject at issue. The motion implies that there is to be a distinction drawn and that the principle of the Bill in drawing that distinction is a correct principle. I believe nobody will gainsay that fact. The market reports for years have drawn a distinction between creamery and dairy butter, but, there is no definition as to where the line should be drawn at what is creamery and what is dairy butter. It is perfectly true that there is a good deal of dairy butter which is made just as well as creamery butter and which is of just as high a Quality.
However, especially in the export trade there is a standard of creamery butter and a standard of dairy butter. All this Bill proposes to do is to draw the line where creamery butter and dairy butter are divided at the place of manufacture. In reply to the objections that have been taken as to the number of fifty cows, I may say that figure was adopted after considerable discussion and consideration and it is based to a certain extent on the fact that that Mr. SPROULE.
figure has already been defined in Acts of this kind. In Manitoba a local Act declares that a creamery shall be a place where the milk of more than fifty cows is made into butter, and in New Zealand, there is a similar law. My hon. friend from Halton need not fear that this law will interfere with the establishment of creameries. No man would put money into the establishment of a creamery unless he believed that he would get more than fifty cows milk. As a general rule, about 200 cows is the least number on which a creamery is started. We have to obviate giving latitude for a larger amount of dairy butter being marked as creamery butter. When first class dairy butter is marked creamery butter, no evil arises, but when inferior dairy butter or, repacked butter is shipped as creamery there is a decided danger to our export trade. Therefore some line of demarcation is necessary. There is no question but that where a farmer has fifty cows, he must be a superior farmer and his business would justify the employment of the best appliances and skill so that the chances are a hundred to one that the product of his dairy will be equal to creamery butter. On the other hand, where a farmer has a small number of cows it is just possible the standard of his butter may be sometimes doubtful. Therefore these large private dairies may be safely allowed to mark their butter ' creamery,' while the same rule would not apply to smaller dairies. When a man with a few cows really makes first class butter, in ninety-nine cases out of one hundred, he has a special local market and sells his butter on the reputation of his own name and not as creamery butter, and sometimes he gets a higher price for it than the price for export creamery butter. He will not suffer any detriment by this clause. I would strongly recommend the committee not to adopt any figure lower than ' fifty.'

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I cannot conceive what advantage would be gained by lowering the number of ' fifty ' to ' twenty-five.'

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: You are not a farmer.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I am not a farmer ? I handle more butter than you ever saw.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: You do not make more than I do.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
Yes, I have made more than you ever saw. The fact of the matter is that no creamery is carried on with a smaller number than fifty cows. There is no money in it. The creamery butter is the butter that is exported and not the dairy butter. The dairy butter is very largely sold in the locality in which it is made. In fact in the rural districts it is almost impossible for the farmers to get butter to supply home consumption. Where cheese factories are numerous they have

scarcely butter enough to supply the home demand. This butter therefore does not come into competition with creamery butter. The manufacturer of creamery butter has his own brand and he labels his butter by the name of the factory so that if his butter; is really good, he has the reputation of producing a first class article and he sells his butter at a higher price. If you reduce the number below ' fifty ' it would open the door for every one who thought that they had a fancy article to_ try and label it as creamery butter. No" good would come from reducing the number below fifty.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: The Minister of Agriculture must realize that it is not the number of cows that makes the quality of the butter so much as the process by which the butter is made. There is no argument In the contention of the hon. member for Renfrew (Hr. Wright), who says that it would not pay to run a creamery with less than 200 cows. I admit that, because in the running of a creamery you have to hire all the labour whereas a farmer who has twenty-five or thirty cows utilizes the labour of his family, and he can produce just as good butter as creamery butter if he makes it under the same process. In my own locality we have a factory and when it is running on cheese the milk is made into cheese, and as soon as the factory closes the cream goes to the creamery. How could any cream be in as good condition after it is drawn six or seven miles to the creamery, as it would be if the farmer made his own milk into butter by the creamery process in his own dairy ? This very fact should show the minister or anybody else that cream that is taken six or seven miles and churned in cans on the journey cannot be in as good condition as the milk that is made by the same process on your own farm. When the Experimental Farm was first established and creamery butter was first made there, they never had fifty cows on that farm, and yet I do not think that the Minister of Agriculture would want his butter branded as inferior to creamery butter although he did not have fifty cows. I would say to my hon. friend from Renfrew (Mr. Wright) with his boasted argument that he has made more butter than ever I have seen, that I did not know what made him such a sleek looking man ; it is the amount of grease he handles. I want him to be careful in making his butter that some of his whiskers do not fall into it.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Cochrane) does not seem to know there are creameries which manufacture butter from milk. Every creamery' does not gather in the cream and manufacture the butter from that, but there are a large number of creameries that take the milk and manufacture it into first class butter. It is the creamery butter that brings the highest price. It is
the creamery butter made in the Renfrew creamery that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cochrane) eats in the restaurant and finer butter you cannot find anywhere. It is the creamery butter made in the Renfrew creamery that His Royal Highness ate on the train going to Vancouver, and better butter he could not eat.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Do you make butter out of skim milk ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: No, we do not make butter out of skim milk, or otherwise I would not be so sleek.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: The fourth section of the Bill, which refers to the percentage of water in butter, applies to all butter, whether made in a creamery or in a dairy. I think that should be amended so as to apply only to creamery or dairy butter where there are over fifty cows.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: If butter made in a dairy is made by the same process as butter made in a creamery,, it seems to me it should be called creamery butter. I happen to know where there are farmers' wives and daughters who make butter which is just as palatable and which commands as high a price as any creamery butter, and it seems to me that farmers who have twenty or twenty-five cows, and who make a first-class sample of dairy butter, should not be handicapped because they have not fifty cows as the Bill calls for. They should have the privilege of calling it creamery butter if they have the proper facilities for making it. I think the number of cows for creamery butter should be reduced to twenty-five.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I agree with what the hon. .member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) has said. I think it is right that butter which is not made by the latest process should be called dairy butter; but, if a farmer has twenty or twenty-five cows and uses cream separators in making butter, I think be should be allowed to call it creamery butter. In my section of the country that is generally the case. I would like the hon. minister to explain to the House how this process butter is made. In the United States, while oleomargarine and but-terine are heavily taxed, there is only a small tax on process butter. I think the House should understand all about it.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I would ask the hon. gentleman to leave that aside until we decide upon the number of cows for a creamery. What I said a few minutes ago in reply to the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) covers the point raised by the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson). Nobody knows better than I do that a number of private dairies make first-class butter, as good as creamery butter. At the same time, the market reports show that creamery butter commands a price which dairy butter does not.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
I move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again to-day. There is an intimation that an announcement is to he made to the House from the Senate.
Progress reported.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.

speechtext: House again in committee on Bill (No. 207) to prohibit the importation, manufacture or sale of adulterated, process or renovated butter, oleomargarine, butterine. or other substitutes for butter ; and to prevent the improper marking of butter.-The Minister of Agriculture.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
I understand that we are on section 3 subsection A. I move as amendment to that:
' Creamery butter ' means "butter made by the ordinary creamery process, including the separation of the cream from the milk when fresh by the cream separator.
It seems to me that this is really the origin of creamery butter-the use of the cream separator. Whether there are many cows or few, if the butter is made upon the same principle and by essentially the same methods as the creamery uses, it ought not to be stamped with a name indicative of inferiority. This will affect a great many farmers who use the modern methods of making butter, including the use of the cream separator. Having ten, fifteen or twenty cows, they use the creamery appliances and the creamery methods. They send their sons and daughters to the Experimental Farm to receive instructions in making butter ; and these young people come home and, when they engage in making butter on the farm, they follow the same lines as are followed in the creamery, have their dairies arranged in the same way and produce an article often as good as the creamery butter. They ought not to be compelled to call their butter by a name which will mark it as inferior to creamery butter and so reduce it in value by from two to four cents a pound.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
I was going to move an amendment on exactly the same lines as that of the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule). As his covers the ground so well, I shall not present mine. It seems to me that creamery butter is simply butter made from cream separated from the milk while it is sweet and manufactured at once into butter by the process followed in large factories. A definition of it such as the hon. member for East Grey has given seems to me far better than a definition based upon the number of cows kept. It would not matter if a man had only five cows, so long as the butter was made after the process approved of being the best The

definition of ' creamery,' it seems to me, ought to be one which would indicate the manufacture, not necessarily the number of cows that are kept.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I do not see that the amendment moved by the hon. member tor East Grey (Mr. Sproule) and supported by the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Smith) quite meets the case. These hon. gentlemen say that the process is the same as the creamery process, but it is not quite the same. The creamery is a large institution with everything up-to-date. It is distinct from a smaller concern, even if it be of the same kind, where they have not the some appliances and facilities. The process may be the same, but they have not the same facilities for carrying it out. Now, these creameries have succeeded the old dairy system, they have come out from the old style dairy and introduced this new system called the creamery system. By reason of tills improved system, they have increased the price of butter, and are in a position to pay the farmers more for their cream. If so much good has come out of this process, as X believe it lias, we ought to preserve all there is of good in it, and should be careful about allowing those who are in the old style dairy business to work under it. If the creamery people have gone out and made a superior brand, why should they not have the benefit of it? The farmers cannot complain. They have always called their butter dairy butter, and the mere use of the separator on a farm does not make a dairy into a creamer^, to my mind. The definition of the hon. minister is not a systematic definition, but I would prefer it to that proposed by the hon. member for East Grey.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: What would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) propose, if he does not agree with this amendment ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I cannot accept this amendment, and I would prefer what the hon. minister has proposed, though it is not a systematic definition.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: What would the hon. gentleman prefer ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I would leave it as it is in the Bill, rather than accept the amendment.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I think that the difficulty with the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) is that he is not aware of the fact that hundreds of cream separators are being sold to-day and that farmers own them.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Oh, yes, I am. But what you say does not enable them to make creamery butter.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
They make it on the same principle. They put in a supply of ice, they send their children to be instructed in Mr. SMITH (Wentworth).
the manufacture and they have their butter made in exactly the same way as it is made in the co-operative factories. But when they bring that butter to the market they are offered a price perhaps from two to four cents below that of creamery butter. The purchaser will tell them it is only dairy butter and will refer them to the prices in the daily papers, showing creamery butter so many cents a pound higher than dairy. 1 do not see why we should put an embargo on the individual farmer, when he is prepared to adopt the modern methods and make butter exactly as it is made in the large creameries, using care and intelligence in carrying out the process and making an article equal in quality with the other, so far as an expert can determine. By this Bill, we are going to put a stigma on that butter and reduce it in price as compared, it_ may be, with butter made by the same process on the farm alongside his own.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: It seems to me that some way out of the difficulty might be found by the hon. minister. It is clear that it is going to be a difficult matter to define creamery so as to include all creamery butter and exclude the product of private dairies. The point on which the hon. member for East Grey has based his amendment is the use of the creamery separator. Of course, the cream separator is used in all creameries ; but I hardly think that one would undertake to define the whole process of the manufacture of creamery butter as the use of the cream separator in separating the dream from the milk. That would not satisfactorily define the creamery process, which involves the use of milk in such large quantities that it can be used as soon as it has reached the proper point of ripening. In a private dairy, the milk must be accumulated and the churning must be delayed so long that it is impossible to make butter of the gilt-edge quality that is turned out from the creamery. It has occurred to hie, and I offer it as a suggestion to the hon. minister, that, possibly, the difficulty might be got over by making another grade. Instead of separating all into creamery and dairy, it would be better to recognize the efforts put forth by the farmers in procuring modern appliances and making butter by the best process, so that, in some instances, it is quite equal to the creamery butter. A second-class might be made called 'private creamery' or 'small creamery.' This would provide for the product of comparatively small dairies in which the creamery process is used as nearly as it can be reached by the small farmers.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
The hon. minister would have us define creamery butter as that made in a place where the milk of not less than fifty cows is used. In order to make it correct, it would be better that the term ' creamery ' should be defined as a process deserving the name, and give them two classes of creamery butter, one the co-opera-

tive and the other the private creamery butter. This would define it exactly as it is. The manufacture is by the same process as that used in the co-operative creamery, and it deserves the name ' creamery ' as much as the other though fewer cows may be used. While X am on my feet, I would like to ask the hon. minister the meaning of the term ' cow ' in the Bill. The hon. minister bases this upon fifty cows, does he mean fifty head, or does he mean fifty times so much milk. In the management of our butter and cheese factories throughout the country the term ' cow ' has been known and understood as 3,000 pounds of milk. That has been the term used and understood for forty years.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
X think the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) has probably come the nearest to the mark of any of the speakers in providing for the classification of butter. As an hon. member pointed out, it would not pay to run a creamery where you had the milk of less than fifty cows, that is what is known as a creamery. Clause (d) says that creamery butter means butter which is manufactured in a creamery. As has been pointed out, there are many farmers in the country who have not more than from twenty to forty cows. Under these circumstances, that class of people would be very well protected by calling their places private creameries. It is true, as the hon. member for East Gery (Mr. Sproule) has pointed out, that there are not only hundreds, but thousands of cream separators in use throughout this country. The milk is taken warm from the cow, and the cream is extracted by separators, and that cream is precisely of the same quality as is used in the larger creamery. But probably there may not be enough cream for that day's churning, hence it is held over till the next day, the result being that the cream thus held over, while it is very good, is not exactly the same as cream from the large creamery, which is manufactured on the day it is separated. I had the pleasure of going into a dairy last year, where I think they had an output of about 500 pounds of butter a week. It was beautiful butter, I had the pleasure of tasting it, and I am sure it was as nice as any creamery butter could be. But to my mind you could not designate that as a butter factory, or creamery. It seems to me there should be a sharp distinction drawn between the two, and that it would not be at all detrimental to the dairy interests if dairy butter were described as butter which is manufactured in a dairy. I am sure there is not a member of this House who wishes in any way to detract from the reputation of dairy butter. I have been ^buying dairy butter for probably twenty-five years, over the counter in my store, dealing with farmers and their wives nearly all my life. Under these circumstances, I have purchased a great deal of butter, and I have noticed during
the last few years, say the last ten or fifteen years, a very material advance in the quality of butter produced by the farmers. There are many dairies in our section which are up-to-date, and have nearly all the requirements of a creamery, and turn out a magnificent article which goes direct to the large centres for consumption. Those people should be protected by making, as the member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) suggests, another class of butter called home creamery, or private creamery butter.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I come from a dairy county and know some thing about butter making. I quite agree with the members who think there ought to be a third class established. If that were done, I think that to constitute a butter factory the number of cows should be raised very much higher than it is in the Bill. Those who know' anything about butter making know that you cannot run a creamery with fifty cows, nor even with 200 cows, that is, a profitable creamery. With anything less than 300 cows you cannot run a satisfactory creamery, because the apparatus is somewhat expensive, and you have to keep a first-class butter maker, and pay all the expenses you would in connection with a larger factory. I would suggest that if a third class were made, called a private creamery, for private creamery butter, you should raise the standard of the number of cows which would constitute a creamery or a butter factory. I quite agree with the member for Ontario (Mr. Ross) when he says that the quality of butter that we get from the farmers has very much improved. I thought the hon. gentleman was treading upon dangerous ground when he suggested there might have been a time when every farmer's wife and daughter did not make first-class butter, because with most farmers' wives and daughters it is a very tender subject for anybody to suggest that the butter they bring into a store is not the very best that was ever brought into the market. But I appreciate the difficulties of making a difference between creamery and dairy butter. My own experience is that probably those who buy these articles put a little too high a premium on the creamery butter as compared with the dairy butter. I myself have used dairy butter for the last fifteen years, and I prefer it to any creamery butter that I ever used, and have got it from the same man for all that time.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: It is not spotted butter J

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: No, we make better butter in Canada than they do across the line. I think the suggestion for a third class is a very good one, and I would suggest, in defining what a creamery is that it should mean a place where the milk of at least 200 cows is made into butter; then fix another class between dairy and creamery butter.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I can scarcely agree with my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell) in suggesting a second class for butter, because it strikes me that would tend rather to deteriorate the grade of butter manufactured by a creamery not coming under the purview of this Bill. It would be calling the second grade of butter an inferior grade, and in consequence of which it would bring in the market a smaller price, and would be prejudicial to the smaller butter factories that manufacture butter of as good a quality as that made in the larger creameries. The same method is employed for the manufacture of creamery butter not coming under this Act, only it is made in smaller quantities. The same appliances are used, and the article produced is of a quality equally as good as that made by a first class creamery. Now, I agree with my hon. friend from Bast Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane) who placed the matter very clearly. He said that where the cream is transferred from the farm to the creamery, some distance away it is injured in transit, and would not be as good as that which was made more directly at home into butter. I think that is reasonable, and I feel that we should give encouragement to the smaller manufacturers, and in no way put them at a disadvantage in the market by a clause in this Bill discriminating between dairy butter and creamery butter, which would seem to question whether the butter they produce is first class, by describing it as a second grade, and which would mean a second class price, an inferior price, while the third grade would mean a still lower price. I think that would affect materially these smaller industries that are now being encouraged in various parts of this Dominion. In my own county we are now introducing cream separators, which are making butter equal to anything that can be made in any part of Canada. We are beginning to export. That grade of butter, I fear, if placed on the market and called anything else than creamery butter, would bring a lesser price, and those who are manufacturing it would suffer a loss. Therefore, I cannot exactly agree with my hon. friend from Pictou in having butter graded as one, two and three.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: This is a case, I think, where every tub should sit upon its own bottom, where creamery butter should be marked creamery butter, and dairy butter should be marked dairy butter. There is one thing we have to look to, and that is the foreign market for Canadian butter. We cannot 4>e too careful about the quality of the butter that we prepare for the market. It is a fact that the butter which comes from New Zealand brings from 2s. 6d. to 3s. sterling more than the butter which is exported from Canada. New Zealand butter comes next to Danish butter in the London market, and unless we look sharp and see that we prepare our

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: butter carefully, our trade will suffer. It is very essential to pay attention to the kind of packages in which the batter is sent. They say that the packages in which the butter from New Zealand comes, helps as much to sell the butter as the quality of the butter itself. There is no doubt that there has been a great improvement made in the quality of dairy butter as compared with what it was in my early days. What would be considered good butter for the table then would scarcely be used in the kitchen to-day. We are getting very particular about our tastes. Our tastes have improved and we want high class butter for our table and good butter for our cooking. I have packed a great deal of butter for myself, and I have seen it packed for other people when I was serving my apprenticeship in other shops, and my experience was that the farmers, or the farmers' wives and daughters, prepared better butter for their own table generally than they would think of sending to the shops for sale.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I disagree with my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Ross).

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I am not afraid of calling a spade a spade, or of telling the truth when it is necessary to tell it. I think it would be a great mistake if we were to attempt to brand dairy butter in the same way as butter manufactured in a creamery. The great object we should have in view is to maintain the quality of our butter for the export trade. As to what we consume ourselves, we can manage that pretty well and suit ourselves as to what kind and quality of butter we like.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Considerable good, I think, will come out of this discussion. I am glad to see, while there has been a certain amount of criticism of the provisions of this Bill, and of this clause, there does not seem to me to be any unanimity as to what substitute shall be adopted. I appreciate very fully what my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) a few minutes ago said, and I do not know that I could add much to it, as to the good work which the creamery system has done for the dairy and butter interests of Canada. Anybody who is at all familar with the butter trade, knows how co-operative work in creameries has added to the trade and profits of the dairymen of the country.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
Have the creameries or the people who have been educated by the men the government sent
out, and who have used modern appliances on the farm raised the quality of butter in this country ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: The work which has been done by the various agencies for the purpose of expanding knowledge amongst the dairymen of the country is the basis of all the improvement, but the profits or the improvement could not have been as great had not co-operative dairying been adopted in Canada. I venture to say that if we were to leave cooperative dairying and go back to the old system of individual dairying there would be an immediate decrease of many millions of dollars in the profits of the dairymen and farmers of this country. Therefore, I consider that anything that is going to jeopardize or deteriorate the co-operative dairying of the country would be a very great hurt to the farmers and would interfere materially with their future progress.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: The hon. minister has a dairy at the Experimental Farm. I suppose he claims that the butter made there is as good as any creamery butter that is made ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I think it is good butter.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Well then, it has to be branded differently from creamery butter under this Bill, because the tartn has not fifty cows. It is not only the farmers who will suffer as a result of this branding, but the experimental farm will lose also, unless they get fifty cows.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I am glad the hon. gentleman has brought up that instance. It is an exact illustration of what I said a few minutes ago in regard to the best quality of dairy butter. The Experimental Farm dairy is a dairy. It is not a creamery, and yet that dairy butter sells in the city of Ottawa at a price considerably higher than any creamery butter sells for in Canada. That is the case with dozens, and I might say hundreds and perhaps even thousands of farmers in this country who make butter and who have made a reputation for themselves and for their excellent dairy butter, and who are selling it at a higher price than that which creamery butter brings.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: You say that it sells higher in Ottawa than any creamery butter in the country. If you export that to the old country would it have as good a brand as creamery butter, or will it have an inferior brand ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
It will have to be branded dairy butter under this Act. If the old country market pays more for creamery than for that butter then it will have to be sold for less.

*My point is that dairy butter made in the *way butter is made on the Experimental Farm-and hundreds and perhaps thousands of our dairy men do make it in that way- is sold at a price at which you could not export it without losing money. They can sell it on their individual reputation at a higher price on the local market than they can sell it at for export. My hon. friend from Cardwell (Mr. Johnston) says it would be a great hardship if the butter of the farmers were to be marked dairy butter so that they could not get ns good a price for it as if were creamery butter. This butter is sold to local dealers who know perfectly well whether it is dairy butter or creamery butter, and while to-day the dealers pay the makers the price of dairy butter, they have the right to mark that butter ' creamery butter ' and to export it as such, but the farmer does not get the advantage of the two or three cents a pound difference and he will not get it in the future more than in the past. Because, even if he marketed his butter, under one of the amendments proposed by hon. gentlemen opposite, as creamery butter, the local dealer would say :	I know that you make it yourself and that it is not creamery butter. If the dealer exports it as creamery butter, it is he who reaps the benefit and not the farmer. I am afraid that the suggestion of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell), that we should have three classes instead of two would be a little cumbersome. The trade to-day has an established quotation for two kinds of butter, so that I fear the hon. gentleman's proposal is not practicable. The only reason that this Bill proposes to say what shall be creamery butter and what shall not beJcreamery butter, is that there has grown up a custom amongst certain people, of marketing dairy butter as creamery butter and that is dangerous to the reputation of our creamery butter. The ob-.ieet of this Bill is that that danger shall be averted. My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) proposes.
Creamery butter shall be a butter manufactured by the ordinary creamery process Including the separation of the cream from the milk when fresh by the cream separator.
I quite agree with the member for East York (Mi-. Maclean) and the member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) that this definition would be far worse than the definition I have submitted as to the milk of a certain number of cows being required to constitute a creaMpry. It is true that most creamery butt* is made from milk the butter fat of which lias been separated from the other parts of the milk by the centrifugal separator. It is true that this system is used liy a good many private dairies, but it is not the only means of separation by any means, and it is only one stage in the manufacture of butter. It is just as important that the cream should be properly ripened, that it should be churned at the exact state of Hon. Mr. FISHER.
ripeness in a proper kind of churn, and that other details of the manufacture should be careful!}- attended to. The definition of my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) is therefore not complete by any means. It is true that in many private dairies all these things are attended to as carefully as in a creamery, but the chances are that for general market purposes the product is not likely to be as perfectly uniform as tlie product of the creamery. The chief reason why our creamery butter commands a higher price on the market is largely because of its uniform quality. When a dealer orders a 100 tubs of creamery butter he knows that every tub of it is likely to be similar to every other tub, while if he orders twenty or fifty tubs of dairy butter the chances are that there will be a considerable variation of quality even in the individual tubs. That is one reason for believing that the size of the place where the butter is manufactured is an important element in considering whether the butter ought be marked creamery or dairy. Any definition such as that given by the member for East Grey must necessarily fail in that element of uniformity. I may state frankly to the committee that my officers and myself have tried to get a definition which would Include some such definition as this offered by the hon. member (Mr. Sproule) but we have failed to find one which would be complete, and after careful consideration we have concluded that the definition relating to the number of cows which contribute milk to a factory is on the whole the better one. I am not yet convinced that the suggestion of the hon. member for Halton as to the line of demarcation is better than the one proposed in the, Bill. I grant with my hon. friend from East York that the definition in the Bill is not perfect, but I have failed to find a definition that is more perfect.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: 200 cows would be a better definition.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
My hon. friend would be right if we were able to have more than two classes. The reason the number was limited to 50 cows was so as to include small creameries which in certain sections of the country are frequent, more frequent than is good for the dairy industry, and so as to include a few very' large individual dairies where practically the process, the appliances, and the arrangements are all the same as in a creamery. My hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbach) talks about creameries being started on a very small scale. I can assure him that co-operative creameries cannot be started successfully, unless they have a very considerable number of cows to supply the milk to them. It might be that somebody would start a creamery with from 50 to 100 cows, but if be did not largely increase that number in the second season, his creamery would have to go to the wall for lack of

profit Under these circumstances, it has not been proved to me that a better definition of the word ' creamery ' can be adopted than the one which has been drawn up after consideration by the department.
BRB. As I come from a county which is very largely engaged in the dairying industry, I wish to say a few words with reference to this Bill. As I understand the Bill, it provides that the product of a butter factory, where the milk and the butter fat are separated at the factory and the Cream is manufactured into butter, will be placed on the market under the same name as the product of another butter factory where the cream has been gathered from the farmers and brought to the factory and manufactured into butter, although the cream that has been gathered may in some instances be separated cream, in'other instances cream raised from shallow vessels, and in other instances cream raised from deep cans or cans put in water. I would like, before going any further, to hear from the minister whether such would be the case.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: There is nothing in the Bill to separate the different classes of creameries to which my hon. friend has referred. There are in this country a large number of creameries where the milk is brought to the creamery and there separated and churned. There is another class where the cream is separated from the milk at private farms, and the cream only is sent to the factories. There is nothing in the Bill to provide for separating these two classes.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Such being the case, I would have reason to object to this Bill being passed in its present form. Where cream is raised in different ways, and kept several 'lays before it is gathered and manufactured into butter, I can easily see that the product cannot be so good as it would be if the cream were separated all in the same way, even though it were done by a private farmer. In the township where I live there is a farmer who keeps from 25 to 30 cows, who has a separator, who churns'every day in the week, and who sends his butter to Toronto. That butter, he tells me, fetches the highest price. If this Bill is passed, he will have to label his butter dairy butter, although it is exactly the same as the best butter that is manufactured in large butter factories.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: May I ask my hou. friend in what way this Bill would prevent that ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I do not say that it would prevent it; but it would place the creamery butter at an advantage, although it might he inferior.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
It would be creamery butter, no matter whether the 171
cream was gathered or separated. There is nothing in this Bill to interfere with that,

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I do not think the hon. gentle^ man understands me rightly. I understand that the butter from such a factory would be labelled creamery butter, whether it was made from gathered cream or from separated cream. I claim that the one may be inferior to the other. The chances are that the butter from a factory where the separation takes place every day by a separator, would be better than the butter from a factory where that was not done, but no better than butter from a farm where it was manufactured on the latest scientific principles. I for my part cannot see any necessity for passing a Bill of this kind at all, apart from placing restrictions on the manufacture of adulterated butter. Apart from that, I think butter can be sold on its merits, as it has been up to the present. The minister tells us that the butter made on the Experimental Farm here fetches the highest price. It does that on its reputation, and I cannot see why the manufacturers of butter throughout the country cannot sell butter on its reputation. I think we are going altogether too far with legislation of this kind. The tendency is to place restrictions on trade. We are getting altogether too paternal; we have almost everything inspected now. In recent years we have had the Fruit Marks Act, twine inspection, and the time will come when we have almost everything inspected, even the clothing we wear, to see that it is what it is represented to be. I think we are going altogether too far in that direction.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I -would like to ask the minister if it is possible, by some system of inspection, to give certain parties the right to mark their butter as creamery butter. I am satisfied that there is some butter made in private creameries which is better than that made in butter factories ; and if some system of inspection could be provided, it seems to me it would get over the difficulty and be an incentive to people to adopt better appliances and a better system of making butter.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I would not like to undertake to have inspectors appointed all over the country to inspect butter and decide whether it was creamery or dairy butter. I do not think that would be practicable.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman seems to think if this Bill passes, it will have an injurious effect on the farmers who make butter. It will not have an injurious effect at ail. The time will come when there will not be a single pound of dairy butter made in tliis country. Forty-five or fifty years ago there was comparatively no cheese made in factories. That has been changed and we have now no home-made cheese. The same

will be tlie ease with dairy butter. In my part of the country farmers' wives find that they have enough to do without making butter, and those who send the milk to our factories, instead of making butter at home, buy it from us. You will find that in a short time there will be no dairy butter offered for sale.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: If this Act is going to have no beneficial effect, what is the use of passing it ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: This is for the export trade. We want to know that our creamery butter is really creamery butter.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: At present, should this Bill pass, it would bar dairy-made butter from the old country market to a certain extent.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: There is none going there that amounts to anything.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I think that you are mistaken.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: No, I am not, I know it.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I think that the remarks of the bon. gentleman who has just taken his seat show that the best way to remedy all these matters is to let the market supply and demand take their course. He has proved that, without any special legislation whatever, we are getting out of the dairy manufacture of butter and will soon be completely out of it. It requires no legislation to bring that about. The same thing may be said of butter as of cheese. The manufacture in the co-operative building and the improvement of the quality have resulted in the improved articles securing the full market, so that there is something in the statement that we are inclined to be rather too paternal in our legislation. There is some common sense left yet in the agricultural community, and notwithstanding1 the severe criticism to which we hay-seeds are sometimes submitted, we have acquired sufficient common sense to come out about right occasionally in our life. If we find that we get more money from our milk when we put it into creameries than when we utilize it at home, we are going to put that milk into those creameries, and the butter manufactured there will establish its reputation without requiring the brand of any government. While this discussion has proved very beneficial, it would be wcyll for us to consider more, carefully whether we should adopt anj^jhjjise that would have a branding effecttny class of butter manufactured in tljhoMurrtr.y. It is not the home market that th^tm^. minister is afraid of. He knows that the home consumers would choose a good quality of butter and that it would be very largely dairy butter, which is complimentary of course to the manufacturers of dairy butter. The only reason of this measure is the

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: export trade. The hon. gentleman is afraid of the reputation our butter may have abroad. It does seem to me we might get at that in some way without reflecting on all the butter consumed in our own market. The bulk of the butter made in the dairies is consumed at home, and we should be very careful how we interfere with that business. I would suggest that it would be better to allow this clause to stand and deal with the balance of the measure. If more time w'ere given to consider the matter, we would perhaps arrive at a better solution.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I am quite willing to let this clause stand, and I have no wish to force this measure through the House. It is a matter of the very greatest consequence for dairy interests, and I wish to have the Bill as perfect as possible. The definition in the Bill is the best we could devise after very careful consideration, and if a better solution can be suggested, I should be very glad to know it, but so far none better has been suggested. Before leaving this clause, I would like to refer to one or two remarks made by the hon. members for Cardwell and Compton. The hon. member for Cardwell asked me why this proposal was set down in the Bill. For several years back-to a less extent formerly necessary; but to a steadily increasing extent latterly-this matter has been brought to the attention of my department. It has also been discussed at various dairy association meetings in Canada. The exporters claim that to-day there is a considerable amount of inferior butter which is not creamery, in the ordinary acceptance of the term, but which is marked and exported as creamery butter, and is hurting the imputation of our creamery butter in the old country markets.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Is it factory butter ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: No, it cannot be, because they tell me it is not creamery butter.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Creamery and factory, I suppose, are the same ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: In the ordinary acceptance of the term, yes. Creamery butter is generally supposed to be made in a co-operative factory. This butter does not come from co-operative factories. Just where it does come from, I have not been able to find out. In some instances, I am told it is butter bought in some small quantities and packed into packages used for export. In other cases, it may be dairy, packed originally into packages used for export. But whichever it is, it is marked by the dealer as creamery butter, and is sent forward as such, and our reputation for creamery butter in Europe is being injured.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Is it renovated butter ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: No, that clause would only deal with butter which goes through a certain process of melting, washing and so on. This butter is not treated in that way.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Could we not deal with it that way '!

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: 1 hardly think it would be possible. That is the reason why it is felt necessary we should provide that people should not put the word ' creamery ' on a package which did not contain creamery butter, and therefore we have to define what creamery but ter is. At present the term is wide and rather loose. The definition is generally accepted in the trade, but if one were to go into a court of law and try to prove what was creamery butter he would find it rather difficult. Therefore, a definition is required. The hon. member for Compton spoke as though under this Bill all butter must be marked. The Bill does not provide for that. It simply prohibits the putting on of the word ' creamery ' on a package of butter, which does not come under the definition of creamery butter under this Bill. When a person has dairy or any other kind of butter, he need not mark it at all. He need not mark it creamery butter even if it is creamery butter, but this Bill forbids the improper use of the word ' creamery ' on a package of butter which does not come under the definition of creamery butter under this Bill. It does not impose upon the ordinary dairy butter maker the necessity of stamping his goods ' dairy butter.' For that matter it does not impose upon the manufacturer of creamery butter the duty of stamping his butter with that name. It only provides that if any person puts the word 'creamery' on his goods when those goods are not 'creamery butter' as defined by this Bill, then he comes within the penalty of the Bill, and then only. I think, that, with that explanation, the committee will see that it is wise to adopt some definition of that kind and impose that obligation upon those who deal in certain classes of butter. I am quite ready to have the clause stand for the purpose of affording the opportunity to consider what better definition can be adopted.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
I wish to say in defence of my own amendment that I come from a locality where the farmers have not yet changed their system, but from which large quantities of butter are sent every year, being purchased by the merchants. I think I shall be quite within the mark in saying that at least 10,000 packages a year are sent out, coming from farmers, many of whom are making butter on exactly the same principle as that used by the creameries. And, as the price of butter is regulated by the export price, the effect of the distinction here proposed must be to lower the price 171J
of their butter in the market. For, dairy butter will be regarded as of an inferior quality, and this is against every farmer in the country making his own butter, though many of them make quite as good a quality as is made in the factory. The attention of the minister has been drawn to the fact that the effect of this wohld be that the butter from the farm would have to be stamped ' dairy butter.'

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: It does not force any one to stamp his butter at all. It only prohibits a producer of dairy butter from stamping his goods ' creamery butter.'

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: That is just what I object to. The farmer is not allowed to stamp his butter in such a way as to get the best price, and why that should be thought necessary, I do not understand. The hon. minister says that we have attained celebrity for the butter we turn out, yet he says that a better price is obtained for the butter made at the Experimental Farm than that made in the creameries. I have the Auditor General's Report before me, I find that last year the Experimental Farm sold their best butter at 22 cents per pound, and their next quality at 20 cents per pound. Will the hon. gentleman tell me that the creameries do not realize a better figure than that ? To my own knowledge, several of them do. It is a serious interference with the rights of a farmer to prohibit him from stamping his butter ' creamery butter,' even though it is made by the most approved and modern method in a place of manufacture where they have ice and the best dairy appliances, and where they work upon exactly the same principles as is taught at the Experimental Farm. I see a good deal of wisdom in delay, because, no matter what you propose with regard to this point, there seems to be some object tion to it. I admit that the amendment I have proposed is open to some objection, but I do not see just now how to overcome it. At the same time, I think it is decidedly preferable to the clause of the Bill. I think that if this Bill were allowed to pass with its paternalism, it would stamp as inferior every pound of butter turned out by the farmers of my section. And I am disposed to oppose it. It will do a great injustice to these people, and it is on their behalf that I speak.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
It seems to me that creamery bi tter should be defined so as to include butter made by means of the separator, as in the large factories. In our part of the country a good many people send milk to the factory in the summer time, but in the spring and fall they use their separators and make butter, which is called creamery butter, and which, as a matter of fact, is ns good as any made in the factories, if properly taken care of. I know farmers who fcave from twenty to

thirty cows who put their milk through the separator, make butter and do it up in one or two-pound packages, covered with paper as in the creameries, and it is sold on the market at just as good prices as that from the large creameries. Would it be fair to the people who have not facilities for getting to the factories, yet who have all the facilities that a factory can have and make as good an article, to compel them to sell their butter for less than that which is made in a creamery ? I think it would be an imposition on the farmers who are trying to make a good article and who are really turning out butter as good as that made in the factories. To make a mere arbitrary limit of fifty cows, would be unreasonable. Many people have not the means to keep fifty cows, but they may keep twenty-five or thirty, and they should have the same privileges as those who keep a larger number.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
Before we leave this section of the Bill, would it not be ns well to have some explanation of subsection F, which reads :
' Renovated butter ' or 'process butter ' means any butter which has been melted, clarified or refined, and made to resemble butter.
Section 7 makes the manufacture of this butter illegal. I wish the minister would explain what is the intention and meaning of these two sections taken together. As I understand it, no foreign substance is added in making this process butter. Since the minister introduced his resolution in the House last week, I have had a communication from a fairly large produce firm in Winnipeg, who are making this kind of butter in the ordinary way of business. They take butter that is not good enough for the market and melt it down and remake it into butter, without-as I understand it- adding any foreign material. This seems to be an established business, and I am anxious to know whether the minister's Bill will outlaw that business in Winnipeg and elsewhere. Is that the meaning of the Act, and if so, what is the reason for it ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
Renovated butter, or process butter, as it is here indifferently called, is a rather new product on this continent-certainly entirely new in Canada. In this process, butter, supposed to be of inferior quality, is melted until it is in the condition of oil. While in that condition, it is more or less skimmed, and afterwards plunged into cold water. When it is in the oily condition it is hot, and the process of cooling is made a sudden process for the purpose of getting it in what is called the granular form. It is then washed in milk or buttermilk, and treated very much as ordinary butter is treated in the churning process, and is made to resemble ordinary butter. So far as we know, there is no addition to it of any other matter. But the objection to it is that in Mr. JOHNSTON (Cardwell).
that heating process, which reduces it to a condition of oil, it destroys the essential ingredients of the butter fat which makes good butter, and the result is that when it is made up afterwards by the churning process into butter, it does not contain the essential characteristics of the butter fat which make a good and lasting quality of butter. For the moment, when it is made up, it might deceive even a fairly good expert, although there are some qualities in it which are decidedly lacking. But it has been found as a matter of fact that in consequence of the treatment which is has gone through in the melting process it will not keep as well, and is not a wholesome and palatable article of food. The result is that where this process butter has been largely distributed as butter and under the name of butter, it has tended to hurt the reputation of good butter marked in the same way as this is marked.
In the United States the manufacture of this process, or ready-made butter, has become very considerable. At first in that country there were no restrictions upon it, everybody was allowed to carry on the manufacture just as they liked. The manufacture of it, however, has assumed such proportions and resulted so disastrously to the butter trade of the country, that the United States Congress passed severe restrictive legislation requiring a license for its manufacture and a license for its use, where used in public places, such as hotels, also a license for its sale. They attempted in every way to get rid of the danger which it really brought to the butter interests of the country. At the present time its manufacture is only beginning in Canada. I cannot say positively, but so far as our information goes, there are only two or three places where it has actually been manufactured in this country. If we do not adopt the prohibitive clauses of this Bill, there is no doubt that in the near future the manufacture will expand largely in our country, and we will be face to face with the same difficulties which the people of the United States had to face, and which they were only partially able to overcome by their restrictive and licensing system. If we now, in this session of parliament, adopt the prohibition which this Bill proposes, we will be entirely free from the menace to our butter trade which the United States have not been able entirely to get rid of. I therefore believe this measure to be necessary in the interests of the dairying interests of Canada, so that not only abroad, but at home, our butter may be known as pure butter, made entirely from cream, from the fat or milk of cream, and without having been treated in a way to destroy the essential qualities of ' the fat out of which butter is made. People will say, no doubt, that this is still nothing but butter. It is really not butter under the definition of butter which is commonly accepted in the community at large. Butter

is made from butter fat which has never been melted, and which therefore retains in it certain characteristics which are destroyed by melting. This stuff is made from butter fat which has been melted, the melting process having destroyed certain characteristics and qualities in butter fat which are essential to its proper preservation in the form of butter. I venture to say that if we do not adopt the radical measure contained in this Bill now, we will be face to face with an accumulation of difficulties and dangers similar to those encountered in the United States, and that in the near future we will have to adopt severe restrictive measures which will be only half effective, whereas to-day we can adopt an absolutely effective measure which will accomplish the end desired of maintaining the integrity and good reputation of our dairy products.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I congratulate the minister on the change of heart that has come over him since I first heard him discuss butter questions in this House, when we were considering a measure to prevent oleomargarine entering into this country. If I were as malicious as I was in those days, I would take this occasion to flay the hon. gentleman with his own speech and his own language. However, I have learned to be more kindly disposed towards him, and I will only take this opportunity of reminding him of past history. Now, the minister has not altogether satisfied me where the impurity conies in in this process or renovated butter. This is an article I have only heard about or read about, but, as I understand, it is pure butter fat, there is no other composition in it but butter fat, there is no animal fat in it other than butter fat. It is manufactured by people in various parts of this country from butter that is not suitable for table use until it is renovated. This butter is made over under a process by which it is absolutely purified and made clean of all Impurities, and is a perfectly healthy article, and its manufacture is a legitimate business. Of course, the man who makes butter in a creamery may object to that sort of competition. But if tills article is only pure butter fat, as I understand it to be, if there is nothing added to it, if it is simply renovated butter, butter fat taken in an imperfect condition and made palatable and suitable for human food. I do not see why we should prohibit it. We might brand it, we might name it, we might characterize it; but why a man should be punished for taking an impure article and making it more suitable for human food than it was when he found it, without putting any impurities into it, but taking impurities out of it, I do not understand. It does seem as though we were going a long ways to punish the man who invests his money in that business.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
I do not think it necessary for me to advance such arguments as
have been advanced by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House principally, who have studied this matter with a great deal of care.
