I am much in sympathy with those who oppose the Bill on the ground that it seems to cast an undue reflection upon the quality of dairy butter. I recognize that the farmer is the person to be first considered in dealing with this matter. It is right perhaps that those who manufacture butter upon a large scale in factories should be considered too, but the basis of this industry is the farmer and his interest should be first considered. After hearing the discussion this afternoon and the other day, it does not appear to me that this measure will, for the time being, at all events, be in the interest of the farmer. I think it will tend detrimentally to the farmer, I think it will be found to put" obstacles and difficulties in his way. There is another view of the matter which was presented by the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Erb), and it is a view that I have ventured to present before in reference to the legislation in this House, which I ventured to suggest to the minister in introducing his. Seeds Bill a few days ago. I think you are too anxious to introduce legislation to guide the farmers. I think they have a good amount of common sense themselves. I believe they apprehend what it is they need in order to advance their interests. I believe they will progress very favourably if you leave them alone to a certain extent, and I cannot help thinking that this legislation which is attempted to be introduced by the hon. Minister of Agriculture is not in the interest of the farmer, and is but another illustration of that paternal system of government which the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Erb) alluded to.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is almost six o'clock, but I will say a word in reference to what has been said by the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Lennox). I can only assure him that this Bill is in the interest of the farmers of whom he has spoken. Protection to the creamery industry is just ns much in the interest of the farmers as protection to what is called the dairy industry of this country. I suppose there are more dairy farmers taking their milk to creameries than there are making their milk into butter at home, and the product is greater from the factories than it is from the home dairies, but, still, even supposing that to be the case, nobody wishes that the one should be sacrificed in the interest of the other, and if I supposed that this Bill in any way sacrificed the interests of those farmers who do not take their milk to factories I would not advocate the adoption of its provisions. It is because I think it does secure their interests just as much as the interests of the others that I propose the provisions of this Bill. I will have to say a few words in regard to what the

lion, member for Compton (Mr. Pope) said and. Mr. Chairman, I will ask you to call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
On section 4,

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: What is the British standard for water in butter under the Food Adulteration Act.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Under a recent regulation, 16 per cent of water is the limit allowed without the butter being called adulterated.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Does that include all the moisture there is in butter.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I do not believe there is any other moisture in butter except water.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Fifteen per cent would be all right.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: It seems to me that if we substitute the word ' moisture ' for ' water ' we will come nearer to what is intended. Some butter makers leave a certain amount of milk or cream in the butter which is very injurious inasmuch as the butter will the more readily sour, and in my opinion it would be better to exclude that than an undue quantity of water. I have thought this matter out. and I believe that if the word ' moisture ' were substituted for [DOT] water.' it would exclude everything of-that character. I move that the word ' moisture ' be substituted for the word ' water ' in the second line of this section.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I think that the hon. gentleman will change his mind on reflection. This means water by analysis. We have no standard by analysis of cream or of milk. Cream is a certain amount of water, a certain amount of fats and traces of various ingredients; milk is a certain amount of water, a certain amount of caseine, a certain amount of butter fat and so on. But the analysis as to the water shows water by itself. In practical analysis there is no such term as ' moisture,' but the term ' water ' is well understood as an element unless we go into extreme chemical analysis where the constituent parts of water are resolved into hydrogen and oxygen ; water is the element for all practical analytical purposes. After careful consideration and after the scientific analysis of a great many samples of butter, the authorities of England adopted 16 per cent of water as the limit which should be allowed. If we export to Great Britain butter which contains more than 16 per cent of water it

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: would be condemned after analysis and it would be heralded to the world, not that Canadian butter contains so much water, but that it had been declared adulterated. Our competitors would make the most of that, and hence it is necessary that we should guard our trade against the exportation of butter wTbieh contains more than 16 per cent of water.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: When butter is not properly washed there is a certain amount of milk or cream left in it which is much more injurious to that butter than is water.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
I think that perhaps we should use some generic term that would cover not only the water in the butter, but also the milk or cream which should have been washed out of the butter in the making. 1 would be very glad to hear the opinion of a gentleman like my bon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Maclareu) who is an expert in matters of this kind.
Mr. MacLAREN (Perthl. I might explain that I am not a butter maker, but I think I would rather have water in butter than sour butter-milk. I know that whey in cheese is a very bad thing, and I suppose that butter-milk has the same effect on the flavour of butter. I would like to know from the minister whether up to the present we have had many complaints with regard to our butter exported to England having too much moisture in it?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: We bad an instauce not long ago in which it was declared that certain specimens of Canadian butter had been found to have been adulterated. When we followed that up we were led to believe that it was because there was too much water in it and we do not want that kind of thing to be repeated. It appears to me that when 16 per cent of water is found in Canadian butter, it is left there designedly for the purpose of trying to sell water for butter, and any person w-ho does that should be prevented from doing it under a penalty in the interests of our butter trade. Canadian butter such as we have in Canada will not contain 16 per cent of water unless there is an intention to leave as much water as possible in the butter. I say that advisedly with reference not only to creamery butter, but to dairy butter also.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Was it dairy butter or creamery butter which the hon. minister had reference to as having had too much wTater in England ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I cannot say. It was a specimen of Canadian butter.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
The minister stated the other evening that he had a num-

ber of tests made of different lots of butter, and be found that only one of tbe samples contained over 10 per cent of water. Were they all creamery samples, or were there samples also from a number of ordinary daries ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
I stated that a large number of samples ^ad been collected and tested. In answer to the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd),
I stated that the samples which had been discussed in the Committee of Agriculture as having been analysed on the Experimental Farm were all creamery butter, but there were a large number of other samples analysed which included dairy butter. I find, on further investigation, that there were 150 samples analysed at the office of the Dominion analyst, most of them dairy butter. The average percentage of water in all these samples was only 8-97. The average in twelve creamery samples which were amongst them was 9-39, showing that the creamery samples had more water in them than the dairy samples. The creamery samples analysed at the Experimental Farm, 105 in number, averaged from 12 to 121 percent of water. There was only one sample in the lot which contained more than 10 percent. Out of the 150 samples which were analysed by the Dominion analyst, there were two which contained over 10 per cent of water, and one of these at least was considered by the analyst to be adulterated. My hon. friend will therefore see that the statement I made with regard to the general analysis was absolutely correct, and it is proved pretty conclusively by this data that dairy butter generally contains less water than creamery butter, and therefore this provision implies no danger to the dairymen of the country.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Might I ask the minister whether he is in a position to tell us whether the enactment passed in Great Britain to which he referred as fixing the standard of butter, contains the word ' moisture ' or the word ' water ? '

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: It contains the word ' water.'

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: In view of file large number of analyses that have been made, and that very small percentage of samples found to contain water, it seems hardly worth while to pass a clause as this.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I think it will be an excellent thing for the farmers to know that such is the law; and, secondly; as it is the law in Great Britain, it will be an excellent thing, in selling our butter there, to know that we have the same law, and the people of Great Britain will feel that they are getting good butter. For these two reasons, I think the clause should pass.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Is there not such a thing as having butter too dry ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Yes, nobody disputes that.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
I would like to read an extract from a speech made a short time ago by Prof. Robertson :
As to the amount of water in our butter, Canadian butter has one-seventh less water than that from Denmark. We want to keep our butter as near the line as the Englishman will pay twenty-three cents per pound for-and I say that because a dry butter is the poorest butter you have to eat.
So I think there should be -something iu this Bill to compel people not to have butter too dry as well as not to have it too wet.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Properly made butter will have no such percentage of water iu it as 10 per cent. Loose, flabby butter, that has no keeping qualities, might iiossibly have 16 per cent of water, but no properly made butter would have more than 8 per cent or 9 per cent, or perhaps in some, cases 10 per cent. The class of butter which the Bill proposes to deal with would scarcely be merchantable on the market. The price obtained for it would soon prevent farmers _ making it. You cannot compel people to' make good butter by Act of parliament, though you might prohibit them selling bad . butter. ' It seems to me that it would be better to strike at the quality of the butter in some other way than by designating the percentage of water that may be in it. For instance, people who leave a good deal of moisture in the butter are apt to leave a large quantity of other materials, such as butter-milk, and the Bill does not touch that at all.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Section 5 strikes at that.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
No. that has reference to process butter. The average farmer knows nothing about the percentage of water in the butter, and there ought to be some other way of striking at the poorer quality of butter. Perhaps the price would be the most effective way of getting at it. Section agreed to.
On section 7,

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
I see no string reason why we should prohibit the manufacture in Canada of process butter. When we prohibit ' the importation, of course, we give a cer-5 tain amount of protection to our dairy industry, but as there is nothing injurious in process butter, I do not see why we should " prevent its manufacture. There are farm-i ers who, for one cause or another, manu

 facture butter not fit for export or home 1 consumption, but by the application of the 7 system known as process, this inferior and 5 tainted butter is purified and made palatable 5 and good food for the poorer classes in the * cities, and I see. therefore, no reason why we should prohibit its manufacture. That t it should be marked and sold for what it is, is quite right. No one can question the

propriety of causing it to be marked process butter. I have not had the opportunity of discussing this question very widely, but in any discussion which it has been 'possible for me to have with producers, consumers and manufacturers, I have not found any one who could give any good reason why we should not manufacture process butter in Canada and expose it for sale as such.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: 1 am sorry the hon. gentleman takes this position. He has a large farm and is well known as a dairyman. The position he takes is one which, I think, would be a great danger to the dairy interests of Canada. We have the experience of the United States to warn us. Some years ago we absolutely prohibited the manufacture in Canada of oleomargarine, butterine and other substitutes for butter and I do not think that any body to-day doubts the wisdom of that law. If, at that time, we had licensed the manufacture of oleomargarine and butterine, we would have to-day the same condition of affairs as exists in the United States. Every body who has studied the general dairy work of the world knows that one of the reasons why the United States butter products do not command good prices in the English market is because they have been monkeying with their dairy process. They have been treating it lightly. They have been trying to sail as near the wind as they could, and the result has been that they have sailed so near the wind that the ship of their dairv trade has been capsized, while ours has'sailed forward with favourable breezes to a successful passage and commanded a successful reception in the markets of the world. When we discover another menace to our dairy trade, we should treat it in the shine way. We should stop it at once and not allow it to assume proportions which will make it more difficult to deal with in the future. That has been the case with regard to this process or renovated butter in the United States. They have allowed it to grow until it has assumed great proportions and to-day the United States find that this process butter is seriously injuring their dairy interests.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Is it made out of anv-thing other than butter ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
No, not to my knowledge.
I stated before dinner what I knew about the process, and I do not think that I need to go into that again. I admit, for the purpose of my argument, that it is made out of nothing but butter, or butter oil-except salt; but no extraneous substance. Now the United States have been forced bv the conditions of their dairy trade, with" this article freely allowed to be manufactured in that country, to take action. They have

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
taken the action they took with regard to oleomargarine and butterine; that is, to hedge the manufacturer about with restrictions. We did not do that with regard to oleomargarine and butterine; we took the course of absolutely forbidding their manufacture in this country. The reason that the United States could only restrict instead of prohibiting was that they had waited until the manufacture had assumed large proportions and had acquired vested rights and interests in their country which the legislatures could not ignore. It was only after a struggle of many, many years that the dairy farmers of the United States were able to force Congress to pass these restrictive measures with regard to oleomargarine and butterine, and, more lately, with regard to this process butter. The dairy farmers wanted to prohibit the manufacture of these articles; but, as I have said, the manufacture had assumed such large proportions that they were unable to attain that object and were obliged to be content with restrictions and licenses and the hedging about of the traffic, instead of its prohibition. We have been more fortunate with regard to oleomargarine and butterine, and I hope we shall be equally fortunate in our action with regard to process butter. Our experience with regard to oleomargarine and butterine has been extremely satisfactory, and I venture to hope that the House will immediately, without cavil and without dissent, take the same course with regard to this matter, and at once prohibit the manufacture of process butter in this country. I will go further and say that, judging from what I have heard and read with regard to the discussion of the question in the United States, the manufacture of process butter is just as great a menace to the true butter trade of the country as was the mauufacutre of oleomargarine'and butterine. The request to mark process butter ns process butter and allow it to go forth marked with the name of Canada, ns all butter from Canada must go forth, is a very insidious proposition. But the adoption of that course would tend to the destruction of our dairy trade. That process butter will go into the English market labelled as Canadian process butter ,if you like. But the consumers will not consider the difference between ordinary Canadian butter and Canadian process butter, but will confuse the two, and the discredit which will attach to Canadian process butter will affect the reputation of all our butter. In the United States, they require that skimmed cheese and filled cheese shall be marked as skimmed or filled cheese. But when it is sold in England, or elsewhere, it is known as American cheese. When a person gets a piece of that and eats it as American cheese, he is apt to say : ' This is poor stuff, and I do not want any more of it.' The next time he is offered even full-milk American cheese, he is likely to say :

11 tasted some American cheese the other day; I don't want any more.' The grocer may say : ' That was skimmed cheese, but this is full-milk cheese.' The customer will reply : ' X don't want to eat cheese from a country where they skim their milk to make cheese; I do not know what I am getting.' In Canada, there is no skim cheese, no oleomargarine or butterine, so that in the English market, when they And cheese or butter marked 'Canada,' they know that it is a pure article made from the full milk. As long ns that is the case, our products will stand in the high position they now occupy. But. if we allow anything like this process butter to be distributed it will not be very long before our dairy interest will suffer; and the reason for it, will be easy to understand.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I agree with a great deal of what the hon. minister (Hon. Mr. Fisher) has said. If we prevent the manufacture of this process butter there will be no market for bad butter, and it will have to rank as soap grease-

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Rank butter.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
Yes ; rank butter as soap grease. If we pass this law. there will be no encouragement to our farmers to make bad butter. The thing to do is to stop the making of bad butter, not to rectify it after it is made. Butter melted is not butter, and is not a suitable food product and ought not to be allowed to be sold in the markets of this country.
On section 9,
No person shall sell or offer, expose or have ill his possession for sale, any butter contained in any box, package or wrapper upon which the word ' creamery,' or any combination of words which includes the word ' creamery,' is branded or marked, unless the butter contained in the box, package or wrapper consists wholly of creamery butter manufactured at one place.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I do not find in this Bill anything providing that the name of the factory shall appear upon the package. That seems to me very important. for if the name does not appear, it will not be possible to trace packages of butter not made in accordance with the Act, back to their source, and there will be no means of bringing to task those who seek to evade the Act. I would suggest that the following words be added at the end of this section ; ' And is marked in a plain and indelible manner with the name and address of the creamery where made.' This provision has betn found necessary in the Fruit Marks Act, and I see the hon. minister has made provision for it in the Seeds Control Act. It seems equally necessary in this case.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Smith, Wentworth) has brought up a question which was very thoroughly discussed in this House a few years ago, when the Act was passed for the registration of creameries. That Act was designed to enable creameries to be registered and have a number which could be put upon packages sent out, the number being a registered trade mark under provisions for that purpose. The proposition now put forward was thoroughly discussed, not only in the House, but in the dairy association meetings throughout the length and breadth of the country. The trade and the people who were engaged in the creamery work objected to that provision of the Bill, and it was left out when the Bill was made law. I am not aware that any change of mind has come to the people interested in the trade. The hon. gentleman has referred to several other Bills to which that provision applies. But in the case of these Bills, as in the case of the Creamery Registration Bill, the provisions were discussed by the people interested and the Bills were made in accordance with the decision come to. In this case we follow the opinion expressed in the dairy association.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
There may have been other reasons why the creamery-men did not want their name upon the packages. But really I do not see how it is possible that any creamery should be ashamed, so ashamed of their package that they would not be willing to have their name branded upon the package. It is the only means possible of carrying out the Act effectively.
On section 10,
Every person who, by himself or through tho agency of another person, violates any of the provisions of this Act, shall, for each offence, upon summary conviction, be liable to a fine not exceeding four hundred dollars, and not loss than ten dollars, together with the costs of prosecution, and, in default of payment of such fine and costs, shall be liable to imprisonment, with or without hard labour, for a term not exceeding three months, unless such fine and the costs of enforcing it are sooner paid.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Does not the minister think that the maximum of $400 is too great-a difference between $10 and $400. A person might do that innocently in the first instance. I would be in favour of a fair fine. But the minister will see that that fine may be made $400 for the first offence as well as for the second.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: The idea of putting the maximum at that figure is because violations of some provisions of this Act are most serious offences and must be deliberate and intentional, while other offences are comparatively trifling. Therefore, a wide margin had to be left between the maximum and the minimum. The judge will take these cases into consideration.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
You had better make the larger penalty apply to the manufacture

of process butter, and the smaller apply to the farmer who might be running what he required as a private creamery. You say ' every person who, by himself or through the agency of another person, violates any of the provisions of this Act' may be fined from $10 to $400. That seems an awful penalty to impose upon an individual who merely puts the word ' creamery ' upon his butter which he regarded as equal in every respect to creamery butter, and as having been manufactured in the same way.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I do not think it is fair that the first fine may be as large as the second. X believe in gradation of punishment. For example, I would put the high fine on any person who violated sections 5 and 0, who continues deliberately to mix acid, alkali, chemical or any other substance with his butter. I have seen acts of this kind where spite or something else led to complaints, and the judge had been induced to impose the fine.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: It would be left to the discretion of the magistrate to fix the fine. He would take all these things into consideration.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
He will keep within the four corners of the statute, if he is inclined to be hard.
On section 11,

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I would like to ask tlie minister with reference to these words ' any person charged with the enforcement of this Act.' I presume that has reference to inspectors that will be appointed under the Act to see that its provisions are carried out. Is it the intention to have an inspector in every municipality, or how many inspectors will he have throughout the country for the purpose of enforcing the provisions of this Act ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
It is not the intention of the department to appoint any inspectors, except perhaps to give power under this Act to certain officers now in the department to take steps in regard to it.
On section 13,
No appeal shall lie from a conviction under this Act except to a superior, county, circuit or district court, or the court of the sessions of the peace having jurisdiction where the conviction was had ; and such appeal shall be brought, notice of appeal in writing given, recognizance entered into, or deposit made within ten days after the date of conviction ; and such trial shall be heard, tried, adjudicated upon and decided, without the intervention of a jury, at such time and place as the court, or judge hearing the trial appoints, within thirty days from the date of conviction, unless the said court or judge extends the time for hearing and decision beyond such thirty days ; and in all other respects not provided for in this Act the procedure under part lviii of the Criminal Code, 1892, shall, so far as applicable, apply.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: You provide that a trial shall be heard without the intervention of a jury at such time and place as the court or judge may appoint, within thirty days from the date of conviction, unless the said court or judge extends the time. Why is it thirty days ? Why put the party to the trouble of getting an order from the judge to extend the time until the court happens to meet ? Why should it not be the next sitting of the court ? If the judge does not come there, you have got to get an order to extend the time.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: The legal clauses of this Act were copied from other Acts of a similar character. I do not see any particular objection, but I believe thirty days is the time limit given in such cases. I think the judge could extend the time.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: No doubt about that, but would it not be better to have it until the next term of court ? Because, otherwise the party appealing must go to the judge and get an extension until the court meets. What charm is there about thirty days, that the ease must be tried within thirty days ? You are putting the appellant to the trouble of getting a judge's order to carry it on until the next term of the court.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I have no objection to that change if the legal fraternity consider it is better. I want to make the proceeding as easy as possible for the litigant.

Section agreed to.
On section^ 15,
The Governor in Council may make such regulations as he considers necessary in order to secure the efficient enforcement and operation of this Act ; and may by such regulations impose penalties not exceeding fifty dollars on any person offending against them ; and the regulations so made shall be in force from the date of their publication in the 1 Canada Gazette,' or from such other date as is specified in the proclamation in that behalf ; and the violation of any such regulation shall be deemed an offence against this Act and punishable as such.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I do not understand about this $50 fine. What is that imposed for ? You have already made provision for imposing fines.	.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: These fines are fines to be imposed against persons offending against the regulations.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: But the regulations certainly contain nothing that is not in the Bill. They will be only for the efficient enforcement of the Act. Why is a fine of $50 put here when we have imposed fines for the violation of the Act ? What penalty would there be for offending against them ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: You have provided punishments in section 11.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Yes, and you are imposing this penalty in addition as a punishment for offending against something that is not in the Act. X do not think the Governor in Council should have the power.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: This section empowers the Governor in Council to pass regulations for the proper enforcement of the Act. These regulations must be entirely in consonance with the provisions of the Act, but still they might provide certain things which the Act does not specifically provide.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Not by way of penalties. This provides a penalty for the violation of these regulations which is not specifically provided in the Act. This section provides a penalty for breaking the regulations. Otherwise there would be no penalty for breaking the regulations but only for breaking the specific provisions of the Act.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Is it the intention of the government to employ a staff of officers for the enforcement of this Act ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: No, there is no intention to appoint any officers who are not in the employ of the de partment. The intention is to authorize certain officers who are now in the dairy branch of the department to deal with the enforcement of the Act.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: I presume that under section 15. if the hon. gentleman deems it necessary, he can appoint an officer or two. It looks to me as if the Bill was simply for the purpose of making places for a few more officers.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
That is not the intention.
On section 3, subsection (a),
Mr. I'OPE. Have we discovered anything that would assist in solving the difficulty there ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: There was some discussion in regard to this and I think probably the sense of the committee will be that this subsection had better be adopted in the form in which it is at present. There has certainly been no substitute proposed which would meet the views of all.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Would it be safe to reduce the number to twenty-five or thirty cows, particularly where there are separators ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
I would not like to assume responsibility for that.
/Mr. AVERY. Mr. Chairman, I think it would be an injustice to the farmers of the country to leave the Bill as it is at the present time. There are many farmers having fifteen or twenty cows making just as
good butter as those who have fifty cows.
I think it is an imposition on those people who have not fifty cows and who are trying to do as well as those who have fifty.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: The matter can be decided in a minute by the chairman simply putting to the committee the amendment which I moved.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: A legitimate appeal was made to the hon. minister on behalf of a class of the community 'which is entitled to be considered. It would be well to follow up the efforts made by the hon. gentleman's department and by the provincial governments to encourage the use of a better system, in fact of the most approved system of buttermaking. All the larger farmers have adopted that system. Another circumstance which is very encouraging is that our farmers are beginning to send their sons and daughters to agricultural schools like the Guelph Agricultural College, where they are being equipped and qualified to conduct as good dairies at home as can be conducted oil the co-operative plan. I think it should be our ambition to do all we can to encourage these home dairies because it is leading in the direction of a better class of farming. After the young people have qualified themselves for that I think it is a hardship that we should pass anything in this or any other Bill that in any way reflects upon the results of their labours' or discourages the better part of dairying which isv being taken up to quite an extent. In the section of country from which I come, there has been a marked improvement in this direction. I have lost some of the best patrons of my creamery, whose sons have gone to Guelph and equipped themselves for manufacturing butter at home. I think we should encourage that. If we can reduce the number of cows I think it would be acceptable to the committee, and I do not believe we would in any way violate the purpose of the Bill or the desire of the hon. minister. We quite appreciate that he believes himself to be in a delicate position in regard to the necessity of protecting as far as possible the quality of our butter produced for the export trade, and while I recognize that I think we can agree in placing the number of cows at twenty or twenty-five, which would prove satisfactory.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
The question -was discussed pretty well and I allowed the subsection to stand for further consideration. There really was no proposition put before the committee which seemed to suit hon. members generally. My hon. friend (Mr. Pope) himself, said that he was doubtful as to his original proposition to reduce the number to twentydive. The hon. member for Halton (Mr Henderson) proposes twenty-five and now another hon. gentleman gets up and says it ought to be fifteen or rwenty. Of course, these are difficult propositions which show that what-

ever the number chosen should be, there will be some objection and some possible idea that a hardship will arise in some individual instances. The object is to see that the word ' creamery ' should not be put on butter which is not made on such a large scale as to bring about the most favourable conditions. If we lower this standard to fifteen or twenty cows we might as well wipe out the difference between dairy and creamery butter altogether.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: In Western Canada there are hundreds of small dairies where they have only twenty or thirty cows and where they have been stamping their butter as ' creamery' for many years. Do not you think that it would be an injustice to legislate so as to prevent those people from carrying on their industry as they have been accustomed to ?

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
How will you establish the fact that there will be not less than fifty cows ?
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) Take a census.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: In the case of any prosecution under the Act that would have to be proved in the ordinary way.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman from Middlesex (Mr. Gilmour) has given his opinion as the result of forty years experience that in the language of butter makers, a cow means an animal that will produce 3,000 pounds of milk in a year. There is a marked difference between cows, because one animal may give 3,000 pounds and another 7.000 pounds of milk in a year. A good deal depends on what interpretation you are going to put on that word, and we should have the opinion of the Minister of Agriculture as to what his intention is, and how he thinks the Act will be read when it becomes law.

maintopic: ADULTERATION OF BUTTER.
speechtext:
The intention is to count the number of heads of cattle. They may have the idea of 3,000 pounds of milk being the product of a cow in one part of the country and it may be totally different in another part of the country, but the number of heads can be easily counted.
Amendment (Mr. Henderson) negatived. Amendment (Mr. Sproule) negatived.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon W.
S. Fielding) moved that the House go into Committee of Supply.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext: j

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext:
This afternoon the leader of the opposition called the attention of the government to the purchase by the British authorities of a large number of cattle in the United States for the restocking of Boer farms in South Africa. The Minister of Agriculture replied that a certain amount of correspondence had taken place between this government and Lord Strathcona and that certain representations had been made. We, upon this side of the House, and many people outside of the House, feel that this is so important a matter that it should have received more attention from the government, and to emphasize that fact I' shall conclude with a motion. Now, Sir, we have heard a great deal on both sides of the water about preferential tariffs, and certain other things that will bring the colonies and the mother country more closely together. We believe there should be something more than sympathy, something more than a deep, loyal, patriotic feeling on the part of the colonies for the motherland, and on the part of the motherland for the colonies. I know of no better way to emphasize that desire than by the government of England, when it has an opportunity of doing business with the outside world, making an effort at least to do business with British colonies rather than with foreign nations. We have only one way of presenting our case before the British government or the British parliament, and that is through the government of our own country. After the splendid position Canada obtained in the British mind, after the close of the war in South Africa, as a result of the efforts Canada made on that occasion to emphasize her desire to maintain the British empire in its integrity, we cannot but feel that if the hon. Minister of Agriculture and the government to which he belongs had put forth a proper effort we should have had some practical results, such as the purchase of these animals in Canada instead of in the country to the south of us. The hon. gentleman told us this afternoon that he had not even heard of this transaction. We remember a year or two ago when another important matter, the purchase of meat supplies for the British army, was before us, the hon. Minister of Agriculture confessed in this House that he had not heard of it. Well, we know that the hon. minister is not deaf, that it is possible for him to hear; we know that he is not illiterate, that he reads; we know that he is entrusted with an important department of the government; and yet it is strange that within gunshot of where we are now sitting, Major Maude, the agent of the British government in this matter, was living day in and day out; and the Minister of Agriculture and the goveriflnent (o which he belongs know nothing whatever of the purchase of this stock. I do not deny it. I am bound to accept the words of tile lion, gentleman, and I do accept them to the full-

est extent; but it is surprising to say the least. We find that this steamer, the ' At-lanteau,' is at Montreal, loading 2,000 tons of hay, and that Mr. Kirtaw, of New York, their representative in the United States, is superintending the shipment. Can it he possible that this has not been known to the lion. Minister of Agriculture ? We all remember what great credit was claimed for the Minister of Agriculture and his colleagues when they changed the regulations between this country and the United States, and claimed that they had thereby opened up a market for our stock. We remember how the flag again went up when they .entered into negotiations with regard to the importation of diseased cattle, and how we were told that the prompt action of the Minister of Agriculture had saved this country. If those were matters of importance, surely au opportunity like this, which was heralded throughout this country months ago, should have reasonably called for a much greater effort than the hon. gentleman seems to have put forth. There could not have been a more opportune time than this very year, when every section of the country from which the hon. gentleman conies has been suffering from a severe drought. We know that our hay crop is not going to be more than 50 per cent of what it ought to be, and cattle are very cheap-just the kind that are best adapted for South Africa-better than the cattle of Texas or other southern states, where the cattle are poorly bred. There are thousands of cattle in our country seeking a market, and surely the lion. Minister of Agriculture and his colleagues could have afforded sufficient time to have urged on the gentleman who represents Great Britain in this matter, Major Maude, the value of our cattle, and thus have secured some relief for the people who have been suffering in the eastern part of ,tlie country. The hon. gentleman says he has not heard that there has been any exportation of cattle from this country. I think that under these circumstances we are justified in finding fault with the hon. gentleman and the government for neglect. True, he has been basking in the sunny climate of Japan, enjoying himself for weeks and weeks; but that was his desire. He went there, I presume, with the idea of doing good to Canada. But I expect that when the time arrives, it will turn out to be like his trip to England, where he was present when the negotiations were going on for the sale of army meat, and yet had not heard anything about it. So, when we come to find that the United States or some other country is getting the advantage of us in Japan, I suppose we shall find that the hon. gentleman -has not heard of it, just as on this occasion he has not heard of the thousands of head of cattle tljjit are being exported to South Africa to the great advantage of the people to the south of us.
It is not my intention to speak longer on this matter; I do not think it is necessary. I have drawn the attention of this House to the fact that the government have taken very little means to urge on the British authorities the great advantage it would be to this country to provide cattle for shipment to South Africa, and to the confession which the hon. minister made this afternoon, that he did not know anything about this matter, though on one occasion he had taken sufficient interest in it to communicate with Lord Stratlicona. Perhaps lie has had one communication, or he may have had a dozen, with Lord Strathcona; but he did not follow the matter up. It would have been more important, if the hon. minister had heard anything about it, to have gone to England himself rather than to Japan.
No doubt the hon. gentleman was an attractive personality when in Japan, but we would have been inclined to look with indulgence on his holiday there if he had done something for Canada. Had he obtained for the province of Quebec, and particularly the eastern section of that province, the material advantage which might have been obtained had proper efforts been made to secure for us the restocking of the Boer farms, we would not have concerned ourselves about that hon. gentleman's oriental experiences ; but I trust that now that I have brought this matter to the attention of the House in the shape of an amendment to Supply, the government will lose no delay in communicating with Major Maud, who represents the imperial authorities in this country, and in taking every possible step to secure to our country the supplying of the cattle required. In the newspaper article describing this matter, .it was said that these cattle are selected very carefully, that many are called but few qre chosen. I have no doubt, from what I know of the cattle of Mexico and the south, that very few will be chosen. I do not know of any part of the world where you will get a more undesirable breed of cattle for the foundation of a dairy stock than in Mexico, Texas and the southern part of this continent. They have no good dairy stock. Their cattle are ill-bred animals, more or less filled with disease. But in this country we have just the quality required. The increase in the business of dairying has caused a wonderful increase in the breeding of dairy cattle so that our farmers in the eastern provinces have a large amount of dairy cattle on hand, which they cannot send out to their ranches in the west where they require cattle for the beef market, and which would be admirably suited for restocking the farms in South Africa, and could be had at very moderate prices.
I beg therefore to move that all the words after ' That ' be struck out, and the following substituted :

This House regrets that the government have not taken more active measures for the purpose of protecting the interests of Canadian farmers and cattle dealers in connection with the purchase by the imperial government of cattle required for restocking the farmers in South Africa.

speechtext:
I only intend to refer for a few minutes to the matter which has been brought to the attention . of the House by my hon. friend from Com-toil- (Mr. Pope). I do not think it requires many words to show that the government has been derelict in its duty in not making a greater effort to secure for the stock raisers of this country that market so recently opened up. We have been told by the lion. Minister of Agriculture that the government sent remonstrances to England through Lord Strathcona. Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that these remonstrances had so little weight that at present we find the agents of the British government in the United States buying cattle fpr export to South Africa, instead of meeting the wishes of the Canadian government which has done so much for Great Britain in the way of preference. Does he mean to tell us that after all these remonstrances, made, as he has told us, through the proper channel, the British government has quitely ignored them. Surely the influence of this government is much less indeed than any one would have expected.
The Minister of Agriculture and his colleagues have, time and again, boasted of what the government have done in the way of searching out new markets for the people of this country. I must confess that what we find now reported in the press- and there is every reason to believe it is absolutely correct-is not at all in keeping with the representations made by the government when they told the people how much interested they were in providing new markets for them, told them of their efforts and of the results those efforts would bring, above what had been secured by those who preceded them in the government of the Dominion. Now, one word with reference to the article itself and the representations it has made. We are told that the cattle are of a high class. Surely, the hon. gentleman will not contend for a moment that the people of the United States can furnish a higher class of cattle than the Dominion of Canada can. I have always understood that the people of the United States come to Canada to get their high-class cattle, and I believe there is a very large trade carried on by Canada in high-class cattle to be sent to the United States. Yet we find that the people of Great Britain are so ill-informed on this question that when they wish to secure high-class cattle for South Africa, Instead

of coming to Canada, where the Americans buy their best stock, they go to the United States whose people are purchasers from Canada. We are told that good prices are being paid. That is just the kind of market the Canadians wanted for their cattle, a market where good prices are paid. Yet, the government have allowed this market to slip out of their hands, I will not say without remonstrance, but without effectual remonstrance. Apparently, they have not been listened to. What is the matter witli Great Britain that, after having received the privilege of our market under a 33J per cent preference, they have nothing to give irs in return of rather they treat us with contempt "! We are told that the southern cattle dealers are reaping a harvest. That is very nice indeed. We ought to be reaping a harvest. The interest of the British government in these cattle purchases are being looked after by whom ? Not by Americans, but by a paid official of this government, a man who is paid his salary by the people of this country. He is actually engaged to-day in assisting the' British government to secure cattle in the United States to send to South Africa, and he is doing that whilst he is receiving his salary out of the coffers of the Dominion of Canada. I say we do not want any such officials. We ought to have men more loyal to the Dominion of Canada than to engage in any such transaction. I do not think it speaks well for Major Maude to be mixed up in this transaction in this way. I think that when he was asked by the British government to take charge of the purchase of cattle in the United States for South Africa, he should have said that, being an officer of the Dominion of Canada he thought it his duty to uphold the interest of the people of Canada rather than those of the people of tiie United States. I do not desire to say more. I think this is a lesson to us to be careful in the future what preferences we give to the mother country if, when an opportunity comes for an advantage to be afforded the people of Canada, we are to be treated in this manner which I might almost characterize as contemptuous.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that Canada little deserves this humiliation-for I regard it, and the people of Canada will regard it, as nothing less than a humiliation. This great colony of Canada, if reports be true, has been feted in England for three or four years past on great public occasions. Yet, when there is any business that can be turned in the direction of Canada, unfortunately for us, there seems to be such incompetence either on this side of the Atlantic or on the other side, that the interests of Canada are sacrificed on every occasion. The remarks of the Minister of Agriculture, I think, shows the reason for the whole misunderstanding. Canada, he
says, was the best field in which to buy that stock. He says that the Minister of Agriculture-with whom I have no quarrel up to the present time-said that Canada was the best field. That was the representation he made to the British government. Is that any representation to make to the stupid and incompetent people in the offices in England ? I understood that we were living the strenuous life on this continent, especially in our politics.
If the Minister of Agriculture had led the strenuous life when he was dealing with this government at home, he would not have used only that gentle language, which, to my mind, invited the refusal that the British government returned to his request. He should know that our great trouble in dealing with the British government for the last seventy or eighty years has been that they have neglected every interest of Canada-they have neglected every colonial interest-until within the last five or ten years. The colonial offices in England and all the high offices there are filled with men who cared nothing about the colony until a few years ago, and are loath to take up the new doctrine of colonial ascendency. That being the case, the lion. Minister of Agriculture, who has visited England, ought to have known of this carelessness on the part of the government service of England with regard to the colonies-barring Mr. Joseph Chamberlain and a few of the great imperial-minded men who have recently come forward in the public life of that country. Fifty years ago, when the history of Canada could have been changed, when the greatness of Canada could have been made to run in parallel lines with the greatness of the United States, we were neglected by the government of England, and we were neglected by the government of Canada-because I am persuaded that if the govern-menj of Canada had led the people here to more strenuous maintenance of their position, if they had led the people to be more dignified in their political life and to demand recognition from England of the status of this great colony, we should not have been in the position we are in to-day. And now when we hear so much about the imperial feeling of England all this should be changed. I am an imperialist ; I honour the traditions of the empire, and I can stand here on this occasion and offer the criticism I offer free from any charge of seeking to detract in any way from the greatness of the empire. I therefore, am in a position to charge against the Minister of Agriculture and the cabinet the absolute neglect of the public interest of this great country. Why did you not talk business to these tu-penny-ha'penny fellows over there ? After sending them a mild and polite notice that you desired them to look after the interests of Canada, why did you not set the cable to work to tell them that Canada was not in a position to be neglected, that we

hold the key to the British empire ? I can usderstand how one of these officials in England felt when the Minister of Agriculture wrote that-I was going to say disgracefully, cowardly, message, and it was a cowardly message to send to these people in England. It was all right enough to begin with ; there is nothing like opening negotiations with politeness. But when their answer was received the wires under the ocean should have been kept hot with indignant messages from the government of Canada, to let the people over there know that the day was past when a few little civil servants in England could neglect the interest of this great country.
The government of this country should be told that the hour is past, this government should tell the government of England that the hour is past, when, if Canada speaks and requests the attention of the government of England to our great interests, a few petty officials in Downing street can turn a deaf ear to our request. Why, Sir, I can pick out mechanics in the streets of Ottawa who would make more intelligent cabinet ministers than those who now run the English government. Yes, Sir, we must understand in this country that we occupy a much superior position to the public men in England. The members of this House of Commons are infinitely more intelligent on the general affairs of the empire than the aggregation composing the House of Commons in England ; and the cabinet of Canada ought to occupy a prouder position than the imperial cabinet, because we have a wider outlook upon the affairs of the empire. Before a man could become a cabinet minister or a member of the English House of Commons, he should be brought to Canada and kept here for five years. He is not lit to administer the affairs of the empire until he has breathed the atmosphere of this great colony, until he has breathed the spirit of Liberalism, the high and dauntless courage Jhat every man breathes who lives in this splendid country.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am persuaded that the government of this country is to blame for the whole thing. Because, being the government, and knowing the imperial sentiment that prevails, why did they not say to the government of England :	You are
asking us to give you battleships, you are asking us to help maintain your lleets, and you must do your duty by us? I say that public opinion in this country is ripe for that,
I am ripe for that, because I do not wish to be a part of the empire unless I hear my proportion of its responsibilities ; and when I bear my proportion of its responsibilities I want to be able to charge any official over there, whether he stands on the steps of the throne, or sits in the House of Commons, I want to talk to him from the same level and the same platform, and I can only do that when I pay my share of the cost of the empire. Now, Sir, I want to

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext:
say to this government, I want to say to these stupid little jackasses in London, that the colonial empire could have been dominant over the whole earth, the colonial empire could have been greater than a 11 the nations of the earth, if these little fellows in England had been big enough to look over the whole world, if they had had among them ten or fifteen men like Joseph Chamberlain fifteen years ago. What would have been the position of South Africa, of Canada to-day ? Why, we would have filled the eyes of the world. But because Joseph Chamberlain cannot infuse a little of his own spirit into the rest of the cabinet of England, and into the civil service of that country, we occupy the humiliating position that we do to-day. When this government found that men so small were running the government in England, why did they not instruct Lord Strathcona to send an ultimatum to the English government telling them that if they want us in Canada to be loyal, to be true to the empire, if they want us to give them battleships, and to contribute to the permanency and glory of the empire, they must stand up and look after the rights of Canada, instead of looking after the rights of the Yankees across the way. This is the humiliation to the people of Canada beyond all compare, that Englishmen should think that there is only one country on this continent, and that is the United States, that Canada is an insignificant country, and that the United States contains and controls all the agricultural resources of this continent. That is a monstrous thing. Why, even the people of the United States themselves, I am told, have erected a line against the Texas fever. Why, the people of the United States will not allow these little scrub cattle from Texas to come beyond a certain line, they will not allow them to come up to Massachusetts or to Illinois, they have erected a line beyond which the Texas steers cannot come. They would have to be shipped out of Galveston if they were brought up north. Yet the British government will be. permitted to go into that pest-ridden and fever-ridden country and buy their cattle, to the insult of this country.
I charge upon the Minister of Agriculture an absolute lack of his duty. Why did he not summon parliament, if necessary, at once ? When he saw this insult was perpetrated upon us, why was not the Governor General interviewed and requested to inform the English government that the time had passed when they could play this game upon Canada any longer ?
Now, I am speaking for imperial unity, and I believe imperial unity could be brought about by telling English statesmen that they have got to control the public men of that country and their civil servants, and not permit them to insult the Canadian government. I am surprised that the Minister of Finance should permit himself to be so insulted. That is not the way

of the true Nova Scotian, to permit himself to be insulted by a lot of those little fellows over in England. Why did not the cabinet meet and telegraph a protest : We are the government of Canada, and we don't propose that Major Maude, or any other officer is going to insult this government. It is a direct attack upon the dignity of the cabinet of Canada. I am surprised that the Minister of Finance did not at once take some means of resenting the insult put upon them by the British government, by informing the British government that if they wanted imperial feeling to exist in Canada, they must treat this country with respect. We are not to be subjected to eternal insult. The colonies have been subjected to insult for the last fifty years, and still we have been loyal and faithful to the empire's interests. But the time has gone by when we will stand it any longer. Since I have been in this parliament, I have endeavoured to awaken Canadian pride. Surely we who are descendants of an undaunted race, a race who dared all the dangers of a new country, surely that dauntless French race with which we are combined, surely these two races, we who are the greatest representatives of the human race, ought not in Canada, after enduring the toils we have endured to make Canada great, to permit any longer the affairs of this country to be run by those little men over in England. True, they do not represent the English people, because, as a rule, the cabinet of England, for the last fifty years has represented no body but the little tu'penny ha'penny men who happen to get into the cabinet by some chance or accident. Recollect, I always separate the English people from the English public men. The public men of England for the past sixty years have never truly represented the feeling of the English people. The people were always splendid and strong, but their cabinet ministers, like Gladstone and Salisbury, have permitted that Empire to be insulted by evefy Yankee, and Frenchman, and German whenever they wished, until the time came when it was dangerous for a man that had spirit to pick up his paper in the morning for fear he might read that some fresh insult had been heaped upon the British empire, and there was nobody to protest. Now, Mr. Chairman, I think the Minister of Agriculture ought to resign at once. He ought to resign on two grounds, first, to preserve his own self-respect, and as a protest against the insult that has been put upon this country by the English government; and secondly, in deference to the wishes of the people of Canada, who desire to see a stronger and more masterful minister in that de-jiartment to deal with our public affairs.

speechtext:
I am sure that the 645,000 farmers of Canada will be surprised to learn what is taking 172
place in and around Ottawa, when they find that the Minister of Agriculture is wholly unaware of a* matter in which they are so vitally interested. He seems to be a true Rip Van Winkle. Last year we had a similar question of great interest to the farmers of the west, in the beef contract. These contracts would have been most valuable for the farmers of the west and the farmers of Canada generally. He knew nothing about it. The business had been carried on in England. We were vitally interested in it, we might have taken advantage of it but we did not because the hon. Minister of Agriculture was practically asleep. Another very interesting item of information comes to our knowledge that practically one of the officials from Ottawa is engaged in a foreign country buying large numbers of cattle to restock the farms of South Africa when these cattle might as well have been purchased in Canada if proper representations had been made to the mother country and backed up by an efficient government. Where was our Minister of Agriculture ? He was away in China . and Japan hunting up markets and allowing the market right at home to slip away from him without any effort to secure it for the farmers of this country. He was away studying the Chinese. He can tell us all about the Geisha girls but he cannot tell us about the cattle purchased in the United States to be sent to South Africa. He is a valuable farmer for the people of Canada. Now, he comes forward and expresses surprise that this motion should be sprung upon the House. He even expressed surprise that such a motion should be moved. Will this not be a matter of great surprise to the farmers of Canada, and will they not regret that the government knowing of what is taking place around them in what the farmers of Canada are so vitally interested ? It certainly will be a matter of great surprise. He had never seen, ha said, a more unreasonable proposition submitted to this House than to say that we regretted what had occurred. Does he not regret it, and will the farmers of Canada not regret it, that stronger representations, had not been made, because we have known it to be a fact that if proper representations were made to the imperial government in regard to anything in which Canada was vitally interested, where they could give assistance to Canada, if these representations were properly backed up, they have endeavoured to meet our views as far as possible ? IVe have many instances of this and on no occasion have our efforts failed where such representations have been made as might have been made in this case. It is said that Canada was the very best field for the purchase of this kind of stock. I have no doubt of that whatever. England only requires to know that. I think that England treats Canada in a much more friendly way than



she treats any foreign country, and she dees this because Canada is her best colony. What is taking place in England from month to month is the best evidence of it. It is brought to our notice in a thousand different ways ; therefore, we are justified in coming to the conclusion that if there had been proper information in England, if proper representation had been made, and if they had been intelligently made and backed up by such force as the government could and should command, there is no doubt but that regard would have been paid to them, that there would have been some evidence of it to-day, and that farmers of Canada would have been benefiting by it at the present time. What do we want ? We want better markets. What was the lion. Minister of Agriculture doing in China and Japan for three or four months ? He was trying to get better markets and yet a market right at home is allowed to go and no attention is paid to it, though it is the best market in the world by our most important products and the most desirable market for the largest class of people in our country. Yet the government know nothing about it, pay no attention to it, but utterly disregard it. I have only to say that I am quite sure that this is another evidence that will bring it home to the farmers of Canada what an incompetent Minister of Agriculture they have. He is the steward of the people of Canada. How has he managed that stewardship ? Has he managed it in the interest of the farmers ? It must be evident to all that he is looking after his own interests rather than the interests of the farmers. He is travelling all over the country every year, he can tell us what has taken place in every part of the world, but he knows nothiDg of what is taking place right around him in Ottawa, and as regards the farmers of Canada, he knows very little. He is asleep when it comes to looking after the interests of Canada, but he seems to be well informed as to what is taking place in other parts of the world. I am satisfied that the farmers will regret and will be inclined to censure the hon. Minister of Agriculture aqd the government for their failure to make proper representations on this subject, and I do not think we are going too far to-night when we express the great regret that we feel that stronger representations have not been made, and which, if made, would undoubtedly have resulted in securing to the farmers of Canada an important market that has been enjoyed by the people of the United States on account of the carelessness, or indifference, or want of knowledge of the hon. Minister of Agriculture and the government.
