speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, il the resolution had read that this House regrets that the imperial government has seen fit to purchase cattle in the United States of America, I think we would have Mr. SPROULE.
had a unanimous expression of opinion by this parliament which might have had some effect upon the imperial government or upon the officials in the home office who have control of the purchase of these cattle. How has this motion been brought up ? It is an evidence of absolute partyism run wild. This afternoon the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) asked a question across the floor of the House in reference to the report dealing with the purchase of American cattle and the reply which was given to him by the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher) was that remonstrances had been sent to England, to our representative there, Lord Strathcona, asking him to protest against the buying of cattle in the United States for the restocking of Boer farms. The hon. minister further said that these remonstrances had been repeated, and yet, to-night, without giving any notice of the motion to be moved, the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Pope) brings this resolution in, regretting the fact that the Canadian government did not make more strenuous efforts to prevent the imperial government from buying American cattle. What does he, or the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule), know as to what remonstrances have been made by this government to the imperial government ? They have not asked for the papers to be brought down. They have given no notice of their intention to bring this motion before parliament so that the hon. minister might bring to the House the remonstrances he sent to England, or the letters he sent to Lord Strathcona. They have given him no oppbrtunity to place these letters before the House, so that we are absolutely in the dark as to what these letters contain. Strong language has been recommended to be used to the imperial authorities. How do wre know what language has been used to the imperial authorities when we have not the letters before us which were sent by the hon. Minister of Agriculture ? The hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley) has given us an oration upon the littleness of the English ministers and officials. I regret that an hon. gentleman has seen fit to make these remarks here to-night. If they were contained in the columns of the New York ' Sun ' a greater insult could not have been offered to the British nation than that which has been offered to it by a member in the House of Commons of Canada. Has it come to this that the representative of the old Tory party, the party that always thought it contained all the loyalty that could exist in Canada, is going to stand up in his place in parliament and say :	Why
did you not send them an ultimatum ? Why did you not say that if you want us to be loyai, support us ? The hon. gentleman says that if you want us to be loyal, buy our cattle. It is absolutely cattle loyalty the hon. gentleman wants. I contend, however much

we may regret that the British government has not bought our cattle, that this government has done everything that is possible and everything that any selfrespecting government could do in regard to the matter. This government did not cringe and beg that something should be given to us, but has asked in a manly and straightforward way that these cattle should be bought in Canada. What are the facts ? I am Informed, that at the conclusion of the Boer conference, when it was decided to supply a certain amount of money for the restocking of the Boer farms, the Minister of Agriculture of Canada communicated immediately with Lord Strathcona, the representative of Canada in England, and requested that an effort should be made to induce the British government to buy these cattle in Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext: What more could the Minister of Agriculture have done at that time? Do these gentlemen opposite expect that he should have gone to England and held a gun at the head of the officials of the British government, and demanded that they should buy Canadian cattle? And what happened? *When it afterwards came to the knowledge of the Minister of Agriculture that the British government were buying these cattle in the United States of America, he immediately sent a remonstrance to Lord Strathcona. What more could any Minister of Agriculture have done ? There is no doubt that it is regrettable that the British government should have seen fit to buy these cattle in the United States. It is to be regretted that at a time when we were sending our sons to shed their blood on the veldts of South Africa, and when we were paying heavy contributions towards the Boer war ; at a time when the people of the United States were singing long live Kruger, and were praying for the success of the Boers, when almost every newspaper in the United States was coming out in yellow journalism fashion condemning England, it is to be regretted that at such a time the British government were buying horses in the United States for the use of the British army. But, Sir, we must go about this matter in a dignified manner. This government could not in self respect have done more than was done by the Minister of Agriculture in the premises. I can only regret that the motion of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pope), instead of being one of censure on the Minister of Agriculture and the government of Canada, is not a motion of regret that the British government did not see fit to buy these cattle in this portion of the British Empire, rather than in the United States.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext:
We have
many things to complain of with regard to
172}
this matter. We have to regret that although the Minister of Agriculture sent a remonstrance to the British government, he did not recognize it as his duty to follow that remonstrance up, aud as the member for Colchester has said, make the cables hot with messages to the British government endeavouring to induce them to buy these cattle in this country. This year aud last year the government have asked for thousands of dollars to extend our markets in foreign countries, but surely they should have means at their hand to be informed of what the British government is doing in the way of purchasing supplies, and to bring these purchases to Canada. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Logan) has taxed the British government with being wrong, but the British government did exactly what any wise man would do ; the British government pursued the policy which has been theirs for the last fifty years, of buying in the cheapest market. And, Sir, if the policy of the Conservative party had been adopted when they advocated a mutual preference, these cattle would have been bought in Canada and not in the United States. The Conservative party has maintained that the only sensible preference is a preference under which you get something for what you give, and if this government had adopted such a preference the English government would be buying from us to-day. There is no sentiment or sympathy in trade. The English people will buy in the best market. It is the boast of this government that as a result of the preference, England has bought more from us than she would otherwise have done, but In this very case, where the British government itself was the purchaser, it passed our doors and bought in a foreign market. Let this government negotiate for a mutual preference which will apply not only to the British Isles, but to the British colonies ; such a preference as has been advocated by the Conservative party, and then we will not have to complain of this kind of thing happening in the future. That is the only way to make trade mutually advantageous.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext:
The admission of the Minister of Agriculture that he was not taken by surprise as to the intention of the British government to buy these cattle in the United States, ought to have given him sufficient time to make out a better case than he seems to have made with the authorities in England in connection with this matter. He ought to bring down to the House the replies which he received to the remonstrances which he made to the British government, so that we may know the reason for purchasing these cattle in the United States. We must remember, Sir, that the British government has had some experience of doing business with the hon. gentleman's department in buying hay and oats, and perhaps that may be a reason why

they did not care to buy cattle through his department.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) is very willing to vote for a motion of censure on the British governmeut, but he is very loath to censure those who are directly responsible for neglecting Canadian interests. We have a right to assume that if the Minister of Agriculture had made proper remonstrances to the British government, they would have given heed to them. But we cannot forget that the premier himself told the people of England that he did not want any return for the preference, and that the Minister of Agriculture, following in his leader's example, told the people the same thing when he was in England. Even a prominent official of this government who figured in political circles-in Liberal party circles some years ago in this country-he told an English chamber of commerce that the Canadian government did not want anything in return for the preference they gave to England. When you tell the English people, on one hand that you do not want anything, and then go back and tell them that you do, they do not know whether to believe you in the first instance or in the second. The position taken by the Prime Minister and by his Minister of Agriculture with regard to preference has placed them in a very sorry plight when they go to demand anything from the British government. Our hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) says he would vote for a resolution censuring the English government. He would not give them any notice, though he, wants notice given to this government. They might have some reasonable explanation to give why they did not buy your cattle. The hon. gentleman's loyalty is not very deep ; it is hardly lip loyalty.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext: It is not cattle loyalty, then.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext: It is on four feet, however, and would leave the country at any hour. The hon. gentleman would censure the British government without any notice, but he would not touch a hair on the head of the hon. Minister of Agriculture. I say there is one of two reasons why the British government have not bought our cattle: either they do not want to do business with the government of this country after the experience they have had, or else our cattle are not the cattle they want. This House has a right to know what reason the British government have given the authorities of this country why they do not want to buy our cattle. The English governmeut over a year ago gave notice in the House of Commons, not only to this country, but to the world, that they intended to restock the farms in South Africa. There is no question that time enough was given to the

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext: government and people of this country to make a case. I suppose the Department of Agriculture is somewhat of an intelligence department, where people who want to learn anything about the agricultural products of this country can find out; but I suppose there has been some miscarriage of duty, and the British government have not been apprized of the position of this country or its ability to fill their orders in this respect. I think the minister owes to the House some explanation of the reasons that were given by the British government. He has seen fit not to give it to the House. He had notice at three o'clock this afternoon, on a question that was asked across the House, which drew the attention of the House and the country to the fact that the English government, through Major Maude, was purchasing or intending to purchase cattle in Texas for shipment to South Africa. The Canadian people have a perfect right to know what reason the English government have given the authorities of this country why Canadian cattle could not fill the bill instead of Texas cattle. They seem to think that the Canadian people are not in a position to fill these orders. It is the duty of the authorities of this country to disabuse their minds of that idea, if that is the case, and the hon. gentleman's department surely ought to be in a position to give them the necessary information. When we asked for papers at the beginning of this session in reference to some business that was done in England through this government, they actually refused to bring the papers down, because, they said, they had reference to business connected with the imperial government-through our department here. That being the case, it is a question whether, when we ask for this information, they will give it to us. I think our hon. friend who represents Cumberland had better transfer his loyalty from the English government to this government, and censure them. It might do them good.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext:
I think, Sir. Speaker, the country has some reason to complain of the manner in which this subject has been brought before the House. At three o'clock this afternoon, the hon. leader of the opposition, on the calling of the Orders of the Day, read an item from a newspaper intimating the intention of the imperial government to purchase some cattle in the southern states for South Africa. My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture stated then that he had caused communication to be sent to the Canadian representative in England, Lord Strathcona,' requesting him to communicate to the imperial government how desirable it was that their purchases should be made in Canada. The leader of the opposition appeared to be satisfied with that explanation, and resumed his seat, without intimating in the slightest degree that either at a later stage to-day or at any subsequent period in

the session he intended again to invite the attention of the House to the matter. And now. at nine o'clock at night, in the absence of the leader of the opposition, who appeared to be satisfied with the explanation, after the departments are closed, when documents cannot be produced, when it is not possible to give the exact language of the correspondence, the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Pope) gets up in the House, and, alluding again to a newspaper extract on the subject, moves a vote of censure on the Minister of Agriculture because the imperial government Is not purchasing cattle for South Africa in Canada. The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson), not knowing the tenor of the correspondence, more than what was stated by the Minister of Agriculture, not knowing the answers except as stated here, regrets that a different course was not pursued, that greater remonstrances were not presented to the British government, that a different line of action was not taken, not knowing what the line of action was. And then we have a wholesale attack on the history of the British government and their line of conduct from beginning to end. What midsummer madness has taken possession of the opposition that they must attack everything ? They attack the Minister of Agriculture ; they attack the government in Canada, a government which I suppose hon. gentlemen will admit has done more for Canada than any preceding government, a government that commands the confidence of the people of Canada more completely than any government before it.
speakername: The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir Wm. Mulock).

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext: It makes us smile.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext:
Yes, the country is smiling under the influence of the government. Hon. gentlemen opposite condemn the British government. My hon. friend, Tory of Tories, the member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley) knows no limit to the attack he makes upon England and upon the history of England. The great ministers who haVe gone are nothing in his eyes, they have all been enemies to Canada and the empire-all Liliputian politicians. He had not a word to say for Gladstone nor for Salisbury. None of the great statesmen of the last fifty years came up to his ideas of a British statesman :	Lord Russell. Lord
Palmerston, Mr. Gladstone, and all the galaxy of men who filled the office of premier of England for the last fifty years failed to come up to his high ideal ; none of them represent his true conception of statesmanship. There is only one man who could have filled the office of premier of England to his satisfaction : unfortunteiy for England, but fortunately for Canada, he is representing Colchester in the Canadian House of Commons. The Canadian government is only incidentally a subject of attack here. My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) asks, what will the 640.000 farmers of Canada think of matters that are transpiring at Ottawa to-day ? Well, Sir. to quote the testimony of one of his hon. friends, it costs $28 a minute for every one who speaks in this House. -Some of them may wonder whether they have got value for the many minutes the hon. member for East Grey and others have spoken. Why, each minute the hon. gentleman has spoken he has wasted the value of one of these Canadian cattle.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext: What about the Postmaster General ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext:
He is very economical of the people's time. He is a working man. When these 640,000 farmers are endeavouring to form an opinion on the proceedings at Ottawa, they will ask themselves this question :	Is this remnant
in opposition all that has survived of the glorious Conservative party in days gone by, which upheld in every shape the imperial connection between Great Britain and Canada ? What will they think of these members of the Tory party in this House who to-day cheer sentiments that point to the disintegration of the empire and the separation of Canada from Great Britain't These hon. gentlemen never fail to take advantage of an opportunity to assail Great Britain because of what they call her ingratitude to Canada. The hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Smith) in endeavouring to explain why Great Britain had not purchased these cattle in Canada said that it was no doubt because of her traditional policy of purchasing in the cheapest market. That is probably the true and honest explanation, but if that be so, how does the hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Broder) reconcile it with his own suggestion, that the imperial government did not care to have any business dealings with the Department of Agriculture. I do not believe, however, that when my hon. friend gave expression to that opinion, he believed in his heart that there was any justification for it, but he merely uttered it because it suggested itself to his mind as something smart to say for the moment. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the
640,000	farmers of Canada will come to the conclusion that the Conservative party at Ottawa must be completely bankrupt when they can waste the time of the House over such a trumpery resolution. Had they even asked for the papers and had the papers not shown that the Minister of Agriculture had done all that could have been expected, there would then have been some justification for a motion such as this, but they were very careful not to give my hon. colleague any opportunity of bringing dowm the papers, because they knew that the correspondence would cut away the ground from under their feet. But what do they care about the facts ? If the facts are against them, so much the worse for the facts. Knowing nothing whatever of tlie facts, without asking for the papers, practically declaring that they do not want to see them, with nothing whatever except the bald fact that England, for reasons of

her own, lias made purchase of cattle elsewhere than in Canada, they propose this absurd resolution-a resolution which really implies a censure on the imperial government. The hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley) did not confine his criticisms to the past and gone but embraced the living within bis range. Major Maude did not escape nor did the one man, to whom of ail men of Canada is much indebted. 1 refer to bonl Strathcona. Is there any man to whom Canada is under a greater obligation to-day than Lord Strathcona ? I need not remind you of what he has done for Canada. There is no man living who has a greater regard for the interests of Canada. Almost every day we have despatches telling us what he is doing for liis country. In the day time and in the hours of night, his mind is ever occupied in thinking liow he can best advance the interest of Canada; and when we put the case in the hands of Lord Strathcona, we placed it in the hands of one than whom no one was better fitted to secure for it the most favourable consideration. Lord Strathcona waited upon the colonial office and urged on it the desirability of making its purchases of cattle in Canada. He made the best case he could, and if he could not succeed, is there any man living who could have fared better ? Of all men he is the one who would have the greatest claim on the gratitude of the imperial government for his many gifts and services, and who has acquired an influence In the imperial councils second to none.

speechtext:
He made every dollar in Canada, and he is more indebted to Canada than Canada is to him.
The rOSTMASTER GENERAL. I am not speaking of the sources of his wealth.

speechtext: No one will believe for a moment that Lord Stratli-cona neglected to use his best efforts on the present, as on all other occasions, to promote the interests of Canada with the imperial government. * We may assume that everything possible was done, and the 040,000 farmers of this country will be of the opinion that the opposition have by this motion and the attacks which accompanied it made themselves supremely ridiculous.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext:
The hon. the Postmaster General has, in a very violent address, spoken of people making themselves ridiculous, but it seems to me that he might better have applied that description to himself. The hon. gentleman lias had considerable experience in parliament, he has travelled considerably in the interests of Canada, he has distinguished himself on the question of the postal rates, he has earned undying fame by that wou-derful postal stamp of his own devising, witli its marvellous text, and yet, with all these advantages, we now find him driven to the position of talking about everything that is not raised by this resolution and avoiding reference to anything that has been said with regard to it, in the hope that in this way he will divert the debate from its legitimate object. But the only thing he succeeded in doing was in making himself ridiculous. But before 1 say anything further with regard to the hon. minister, I want to give the reasons why I support this resolution. When I first heard it put, I was undecided whether to support it or not, because I had not heard the beginning of the discussion, and I waited to hear what the hon. the Minister of Agriculture had to say in his defence. I was greatly aided in concluding to support this resolution by the argument of the hon. minister. It is quite true perhaps that there was not much time for him to bring down the documents, bat when we recollect that, in the course of the speech, he did not venture to tell us that he had made a serious, persistent effort or vigorous remonstrance to the British government, or that he had laid before the British government the true state of the facts, I think that we have some ground for believing that the motion is well founded.
We can assume, I suppose, that the hon. minister would put the case as strongly as it could be put. Taking the case as the hon. minister has stated it himself, has this House a right to be satisfied with the position in which we find ourselves with regard to this cattle question ? The minister has said ; We made a remonstrance with the British government; we urged upon them to consider the question of purchasing our cattle. Why, Sir, we have had, this very afternoon, a declaration from the hon. minister that our dairying industry is a great industry and that our dairy products are equal to those of any country in the world. And these are dairy cattle that are being purchased to-day. The Minister of Agriculture, though very lately from Japan, returned not very long ago from Great Britain. It was his duty, while there, to have laid before the British authorities so clearly that they would not forget it, that in Canada we have the means of supplying them with cattle as suitable for their purposes in South Africa as can be had anywhere. This is not a recent matter, as the hon. minister would have us to understand.

This cattle question began to be discussed and a policy was initiated almost immediately upon the close of the war, as was stated in this article. It was for the ministry then to make serious and determined efforts to bring before the British authorities such evidence as to leave them no room to doubt that it was possible for Canada, and convenient for Canada to supply what the British government desired to purchase. Now it has been said-and this is a point that the minister has not cleared up-that there is an indication that the ministry have not that influence that we would expect them to have with the British authorities. Otherwise these cattle would certainly have been purchased in Canada. How is it that, with the strong friendly feeling that exists between Great Britain and Canada at the present time, with the recollection of what Canada did within recent times to assist the mother country, with a knowledge of the recent development of Canada and the increase of her trade, that Britain goes to the United States to purchase cattle, when we have the very animals that she requires ready to be sold ? There must be some reason that the ministry dare not discuss, that the Postmaster General dared not discuss when he got up to talk, as he did, in a way to lead us away from the issues before us to matters that do not concern us. There is a reason, and it is that the government in Great Britain have reason to believe that they cannot get exactly fair, square treatment at the hands of the government in Canada. If there was any reason that the government dare put forward, it would have been mentioned here to-night. Failing to get a reason from the Minister of Agriculture or from the Postmaster General, strongly suggests and points out that the old question that has been before the British people, the manner in which they are treated in regard to the question of the oats purchased through this government, is still lingering in their minds-and they have no great desire to deal with the Minister of Agriculture again. Now, this is an important matter in view of the advertisement it gives Canada. We have Major Maude, engaged in this matter, and that fact advertised to the world. We have these circumstances to be quoted against the people of Canada wherever we are making an effort to extend our trade. It is little help to us that the Minister of Agriculture has been, as he says, endeavouring to extend our trade in Japan, so long as, in the meantime, the market that we would naturally expect, is not secured, the sales that we would naturally expect to make have been lost. Before I proceed to pay a little attention to the Postmaster General, let me speak of one other aspect of the question. An lion, gentleman on the other side of the House who spoke in a very vigorous manner, was concerned about the question of loyalty. He thought we
were taking an improper position in intimating to Great Britain by this resolution that we wanted fair treatment. I want to say that Great Britain is a nation that loves fair play, that Britons will admire Canadians all the more for asserting themselves and showing that when we treat Britain well, we expect to be treated well in return. If there is an important point to be made in this discussion it is to let Britain understand, by the attitude, at all events, of the Liberal-Conservative party, that while there can be no doubt about the loyalty of Canadians, while we are ready to defend and support Great Britain in any just cause, at any time, at the sacrifice of either money or men, yet, when it comes to discuss business transactions, we expect that if we consider Great Britain as we have done and assist her in a pecuniary way, we will have fair treatment in return. And it is the duty of the Minister of Agriculture and of the whole administration to let the British government understand that we expect fair recognition when they are purchasing supplies that we are able to provide.
Now, the Postmaster General is troubled about the question of 828 a minute for the time of this House. He might take a little of that to himself. I think that if we were to count his speech at its proper value and contrast It with the $28 a minute, he would be considerably indebted to this country. This is not the first time the hon. Postmaster General has twitted hon. gentlemen on this side on this point. And, on each occasion, after referring to the time wasted in talking at $28 a minute, he proceeded to waste twenty minutes or half an hour at the same rate himself. He stated that he was economical. I grant that the Postmaster General is economical-wherever it suits his purpose. He is economical in certain branches of the Post Office Department, particularly where a man is to be ground down to the lowest pittance for good service rendered. But he is not economical when it comes to a large contract being let by the government of which he is a member, without tender and at extravagant prices, to creatures of the government. It is economy in these things that the people want and not that parsimonious economy which the Postmaster General indulges in to grind down persons engaged in the service of his department. The Postmaster General talks about the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley).	He is
afraid that that hon. gentleman is not sufficiently loyal. The word ' loyal ' comes well indeed from the Postmaster General. Why, he is a member of a party which, for eighteen years, went through this country preaching various doctrines which would have led to a severance of Canada from the British empire. Talk of loyalty. He is one of the pillars of this administration which, when the South African question was new, when it was mooted that we should send

assistance to Britain, when our grand Queen whose portrait I now behold-

speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext:
It would have been better if he had said, hear, hear, a little sooner. I say when that grand Queen was looking to her principal colony for support, were they the first ? No, they were the last to consent to send reinforcements to South Africa, And yet these hon. gentlemen talk to this side of the House about loyalty. I want to say that is not a fair way of looking at it. The population of Canada are loyal to Britain to the core ; but if there comes up a question between parties as to loyalty, it will never pay the Postmaster General to twit any man on this side of the House with disloyalty.
Now, as we have had no reason advanced why this motion should not carry, and no reason to justify the government in the attitude they have assumed, I need not take up any more time of the House. But there is another point. The Postmaster General made an excuse for not bringing down the papers. He says, oh, the departments are locked up. It was too late at eight or nine o'clock for him to get the papers. Yet every night we see them scurrying out and bringing in papers within half an hour, if they want to bring them in, but it takes an awfully long time to get them when they don't want to. On this question of the hay and oats contract, they absolutely refused to bring down the papers, and called upon their whole force to support them in denying us the fair and legitimate right we had upon that occasion. It is not encouraging for us to ask for papers from the hon. gentlemen, especially when the matter is of imminent importance. What occurred last night V Why, the leader of the opposition mentioned two cases where he had moved for papers two months ago and they were not yet brought down. I myself have been urging the government for papers ordered perhaps more than two months ago, and it is more than a month since the leader of the government announced they would be down within a day or two. They are not down yet. That is the experience we have had in asking the government to bring down papers.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext:
I believe the resolution condemns the government for not allowing the British government to buy cattle in our country for South Africa. I want to draw the attention of the House to an important statement I find in a newspaper, on that point. I hold in my hand a copy of the Calgary ' Herald ' of June 6th, in which I read :
Another Big Cattle Shipment.
Sparrow & Johnston have just received from Mexico 1,100 head of yearling steers. They ar-Mr. LENNOX.
rived at Calgary in excellent shape, after being fifteen days on the road. Only two head were lost, and these were killed accidentally. The cattle are looking well, and are believed to be an exceptionally fine bunch.
Now, why do not our hon. friends opposite condemn Canadians living in the North-west for buying cattle outside of Canada, as well as condemning our government and the British government for not buying cattle in Canada ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext:
When this debate started it seemed to be an attack upon the government here, before it proceeded far it turned into an attack upon the government across the water. It would appear, from the tenor of the arguments, as though there had not been any dealings between the two governments in the sale and purchase of Canadian produce. I want to put on record a fact that every body in the House knows, that owing to the exertions of the Minister and Department of Agriculture and the government generally, there have been transactions amounting to millions of dollars between the Canadian people and the British government, transactions which could not have taken place hue for the exertions of the Department of Agriculture, headed by the present minister, transactions which could not have taken place had not the British government been willing and anxious as well as able to buy from Canada and from Canadians. If tiie Minister of Agriculture is to be condemned on every occasion when the government of Britain buys some article it requires outside the limits of Canada, this parliament will be doing nothing else from now until it is finally dissolved but passing resolutions of condemnation. The British government has to buy where it can buy best. It would not be fit to control the affairs of the empire if it did not do that. There can only be one reason why the British government has bought cattle outside of Canada on this occasion, when their attention was brought to the fact that Canada had cattle to sell. They bought where they could but the cattle they wanted at a lower price than Canada could furnish them. That fact has been brought out by the extract read by my hon. friend from Burrard (Mr. Macpherson). There is no doubt, cattle required for restocking the Boer farms are not the high grade cattle that are for sale in eastern Canada. A cheaper grade of cattle will answer the purpose, and are probably more acceptable ; cattle which come from a climate more similar to that to which they are to be sent ; cattle which are lower in price than that at which they could be purchased here. Can any one find fault with either the British government or the government of Canada for such a transaction ? For my part it seems too bad that this House should be made an exhibition of before the country, by putting forward such a resolution, at such a time,

giving rise to such a debate as we have heard to-night.

speechtext:
The increase is more apparent than real. In the estimates for the current year we had $110,000 for this service, but we were obliged the other day to come down and ask for a supplementary vote for $60,000, making the expenditure $170,000. The reason I was obliged to ask for this sum when we only asked for $110,000 last year was that this extra expenditure was due, as I explained when we were discussing the supplementary vote, to the continued prevalence of small-pox on our southern boundary in the United States, and to the necessity of guarding against its coming across the line, and also to a continuance of small-pox in the North-west Territories which we have been obliged to deal with, they having no provincial health authorities. The actual expenditure for the year ending June SOtli last was $170,000. This year we found it amounted to $170,000 again, notwithstanding the expectation that the epidemic would die out and that we would not require such a Large sum of money. Now, there seems to be no reason to believe that the epidemic is likely to die out during the ensuing year. If it does, we need not spend this money, but the appearances to-day are that it is just as likely to continue for the next year ns it has continued during the current year. Under these circumstances we think it necessary to take the full amount experience has

shown that we require during the last two years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF CATTLE FOR SOUTH AFRICA.
speechtext: I think if I correctly understood the hon. minister, this large increase of .SCO,220 is all due to the epidemic of small-pox ?

speechtext: 1 said that there was no real increase over the amount expended during the current year at all.

speechtext: That was explained when I asked for the supply vote for the current year. AVe did not expect to require that money during the current year. When the estimates were made up for the current year the anticipation was that this epidemic would die out and that we would not require the extra expenditure. Experience has shown that it has not died out. On the contrary it has continued to be as great as it was last year and there is no indication of its decreasing, or that it is likely in the near future to decrease. AVe found that in this current year we had to spend just as much as we did last year, and we see no reason to believe that we will not have to spend as much during the ensuing year. The increase is apparent rather than real in comparison with the actual expenditure of this year. AVe are only asking for the same amount that has actually been expended this year and last year.
